passages.title: Instruments That Argue
text: It is customary to treat scientific instruments as neutral windows: the telescope merely extends the eye, the thermometer merely registers what was already there. On this picture, theory lives in the minds of scientists and in the pages of journals, while instruments are passive servants whose only virtue is accuracy. I want to suggest that this picture has the relationship backward. Instruments are not servants of theory so much as condensed arguments, and a great deal of what a scientific community believes is stored in its equipment rather than in its explicit doctrines.

Consider the early thermometer. Before anyone could measure temperature, someone had to decide that the expansion of a liquid in a sealed tube tracked something real and uniform, and that equal increments of expansion corresponded to equal increments of heat. These were not observations; they were commitments, and contested ones. Different liquids expanded at different rates, and for decades makers disagreed about which substance told the truth. When mercury eventually won, it won partly because it was convenient to work with, not because anyone had proven its fidelity. Yet once mercury thermometers filled laboratories, the assumptions built into them became invisible. A student reading a scale was, without knowing it, endorsing a theory of heat she could not have stated.

This is why I find it misleading to say that experiments test theories while instruments merely collect data. Every reading is already shaped by choices about what counts as a signal and what counts as noise, and those choices were made by craftsmen and committees long before the experiment began. When a new result conflicts with an established one, scientists rarely blame the instrument first, not because instruments are infallible but because doubting them would mean reopening settled arguments that no one remembers having.

None of this implies that science is arbitrary. Embedded assumptions can be dug out and examined, and the history of science contains many episodes in which a discrepancy finally forced someone to ask what an instrument had been taking for granted. My claim is more modest: the rationality of science is partly a rationality of things. To understand why a field believes what it does, we should read its catalogues of apparatus as carefully as we read its theories.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
o: Instruments are neutral windows that extend human perception.
Paragraph 1 presents this as the customary view the author rejects.
Instruments embody theoretical commitments that often go unexamined.
Correct: paragraph 1 calls instruments condensed arguments, and paragraphs 2-4 develop how their assumptions become invisible.
Scientific conclusions are arbitrary because instruments are biased.
Paragraph 4 explicitly denies that science is arbitrary.
Mercury thermometers were less accurate than earlier designs.
Paragraph 2 never compares accuracy; it says mercury's fidelity was assumed, not proven.
qs.x: The thesis comes in paragraph 1: instruments are condensed arguments that store a community's beliefs, and paragraphs 2 to 4 show those built-in assumptions becoming invisible. The neutral-window view is the position the author argues against, and the arbitrariness reading overshoots, since paragraph 4 says science is not arbitrary and that hidden assumptions can be examined.

qs.q: According to the passage, mercury became the standard thermometric liquid partly because it:
o: had been proven to expand uniformly with heat
Paragraph 2 says no one had proven mercury's fidelity.
was cheaper than any competing liquid
Cost is never mentioned in paragraph 2; this is outside information.
was endorsed after a decisive experiment
Paragraph 2 describes decades of dispute, not a decisive experiment.
was convenient to work with
Correct: paragraph 2 says mercury won partly because it was convenient, not because its fidelity was proven.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 says mercury won partly because it was convenient to work with, not because anyone had proven its fidelity. That rules out the tempting proof answer, which is the exact opposite of the text. Cost is never mentioned, so choosing it brings in outside assumptions the passage does not support.

qs.q: The author mentions a student reading a thermometer scale primarily to illustrate that:
o: users of an instrument can unknowingly accept its built-in assumptions
Correct: paragraph 2 says the student endorsed a theory of heat she could not have stated.
students were poorly trained in the theory of heat
Paragraph 2's point is about invisible assumptions, not inadequate teaching.
thermometers were too difficult for beginners to read
Nothing in paragraph 2 suggests the scale was hard to read.
early mercury thermometers gave inaccurate readings
Paragraph 2 never claims the readings were wrong, only that assumptions were hidden.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 ends with a student who, by reading a scale, endorses a theory of heat she could not have stated. The example shows assumptions passing quietly into users. It does not show bad training or wrong readings: the author never says the readings were inaccurate, only that the commitments behind them went unseen.

qs.q: The author would most likely DISAGREE with which statement?
o: Discrepancies sometimes force scientists to examine what instruments assume.
Paragraph 4 affirms this directly.
Scientists tend not to blame instruments first when results conflict.
Paragraph 3 makes exactly this claim.
Because instruments embed prior choices, scientific results cannot be rationally trusted.
Correct: paragraph 4 says science is not arbitrary and its embedded assumptions can be examined.
Catalogues of apparatus deserve study alongside scientific theories.
Paragraph 4 ends by recommending this.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 says science is not arbitrary, that embedded assumptions can be dug out and examined, and that science has a rationality of things. So the author would reject the claim that embedded choices make results untrustworthy. The other three statements restate claims the author makes in paragraphs 3 and 4, so the author would agree with them.

qs.q: Which historical finding would most strengthen the author's argument?
o: Two rival thermometer designs gave identical readings under every condition tested.
Agreement between designs says nothing about hidden commitments in paragraph 2's sense.
Scientists facing a surprising result usually suspected their instruments first.
This contradicts paragraph 3's claim that instruments are rarely blamed first.
A measurement dispute ended when one lab's apparatus design was adopted, though the underlying question was never resolved.
Correct: it shows a commitment settled by equipment rather than argument, as paragraphs 2-3 describe.
Textbooks of the period stated every assumption built into common instruments.
This undercuts paragraph 2's claim that the assumptions became invisible.
qs.x: The author argues that equipment can settle commitments that argument never settled and that then go unexamined (paragraphs 2 and 3). A dispute that ended because one design was adopted, while the real question stayed open, is exactly that pattern. Identical readings from rival designs say nothing about hidden assumptions, since both could share the same unexamined commitment.

qs.q: Which situation is most analogous to the author's view of instruments?
o: A test whose scoring rubric quietly encodes one definition of intelligence that test-takers accept by taking it
Correct: like paragraph 2's thermometer, the tool carries an unstated theory its users endorse unknowingly.
A road map that has become outdated as new highways were built
This is a simple accuracy problem, not an embedded theoretical commitment.
A microscope whose scratched lens blurs every image it produces
A defect causes error; the author's point concerns hidden assumptions, not damage.
A translator who openly adds her own commentary in brackets
The additions are explicit, whereas paragraph 2 stresses assumptions that are invisible.
qs.x: The author's point is that a tool can carry an unstated theory that its users accept just by using it, like the thermometer in paragraph 2. A rubric that quietly encodes one definition of intelligence fits this. The scratched lens is tempting, but it is a physical defect that causes error, not a hidden theoretical commitment.

passages.title: Monkeys in the Margins
text: Open almost any illuminated psalter from the late thirteenth or fourteenth century and you will find, at the edges of the sacred text, a riot of improbable creatures: rabbits jousting on horseback, monkeys playing bagpipes, knights fleeing from snails, a bishop with the hindquarters of a dog. Modern viewers delight in these marginal images, and modern scholars have often explained them as a kind of licensed rebellion, the place where the restless imagination of the illuminator escaped the solemn control of the Church.

The rebellion thesis is appealing because it flatters our own tastes. We prefer our medieval artists to be secret ironists, winking at us across the centuries. But the evidence fits it poorly. Many of the most extravagant margins appear in books commissioned by wealthy and devout patrons, often for private prayer, and there is little sign that those patrons were scandalized. Some images respond closely to words on the same page, punning on a phrase or illustrating a verse in absurdly literal fashion. A rebellion that the authorities paid for, approved, and kept at their bedsides is a strange sort of rebellion.

A better account begins with how such books were used. Devotional reading was slow, repetitive, and meant to be memorized. Medieval writers on memory advised that vivid, even grotesque, images help fix ideas in the mind, and a reader who returned to the same psalm daily needed something to anchor her place and hold her attention. The margins, on this view, are not an escape from devotion but one of its tools: a set of hooks for wandering minds, a way of making the familiar strange enough to be noticed again.

I do not claim that every marginal image had a pious function, or that illuminators never laughed at their betters. Humor and devotion were not opposites for medieval readers, and a single image could amuse and instruct at once. What I resist is the assumption that the center and the margin of the page stood for opposed worlds. They were made by the same hands, paid for by the same purses, and read by the same eyes.

qs.q: The primary purpose of the passage is to:
o: catalogue the most common creatures found in medieval margins
Paragraph 1 lists creatures only as an opening example, not as the passage's aim.
argue that medieval illuminators had no sense of humor
Paragraph 4 says illuminators did sometimes laugh and that humor and devotion coexisted.
show that the Church tightly censored illuminated psalters
The passage never describes censorship; paragraph 2 notes patrons were not scandalized.
challenge the view that marginal images were rebellious and propose a devotional role
Correct: paragraph 2 disputes the rebellion thesis and paragraph 3 offers the memory-aid account.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 argues that the rebellion thesis fits the evidence poorly, and paragraph 3 offers a better account: the margins as memory aids for devotion. The list of creatures in paragraph 1 is only a hook. The claim that the author denies humor is wrong, because paragraph 4 says humor and devotion could coexist in one image.

qs.q: The remark that 'a rebellion that the authorities paid for, approved, and kept at their bedsides is a strange sort of rebellion' serves mainly to:
o: suggest that patrons secretly shared the illuminators' rebellious aims
Paragraph 2 offers no evidence of secret shared rebellion; it doubts rebellion altogether.
highlight a tension between the rebellion thesis and evidence about patronage
Correct: paragraph 2 uses it to show that devout patrons' approval fits poorly with rebellion.
prove that marginal images had no meaning beyond decoration
Paragraph 3 assigns the images a real function as memory aids.
concede that the rebellion thesis is mostly correct
The remark is ironic criticism, not a concession to the thesis.
qs.x: The line is ironic. Paragraph 2 has just said that devout, wealthy patrons commissioned and approved these margins, and calling that a rebellion shows how badly the thesis fits those facts. It is not a concession, and it does not hint that patrons were secretly rebellious. It treats the patronage evidence as working against any rebellion at all.

qs.q: According to the passage, medieval writers on memory recommended:
o: reading a psalm only once to preserve its freshness
Paragraph 3 says devotional reading was repetitive, returning to the same psalm daily.
vivid and even grotesque images to help fix ideas in the mind
Correct: paragraph 3 states this advice directly.
removing images from books meant for serious study
Paragraph 3 says images were recommended, not removed.
restricting illustrations to scenes from scripture
Paragraph 3 endorses grotesque images, not only scriptural scenes.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 says medieval writers on memory advised that vivid, even grotesque, images help fix ideas in the mind. This is a detail question, so the answer has to be stated in the text. Paragraph 3 also says devotional reading was repetitive and daily, which rules out reading a psalm only once.

qs.q: Which discovery would most weaken the author's argument?
o: Further margins that pun on words written on the same page
Paragraph 2 cites such puns as evidence for the author's view.
More extravagant margins in books made for private prayer
Paragraph 2 already uses this pattern to support the author.
Some marginal images that were clearly meant to be funny
Paragraph 4 concedes humor and says it coexisted with devotion.
Records showing devout patrons often demanded that offensive marginal images be scraped away
Correct: this contradicts paragraph 2's claim that patrons approved of and were not scandalized by the margins.
qs.x: The author's case against rebellion rests on paragraph 2: devout patrons paid for and approved the margins and were not scandalized. Records of patrons demanding that offensive images be scraped away would attack that premise directly. Funny images do not weaken the argument, since paragraph 4 already grants that humor and devotion went together.

qs.q: The author's attitude toward scholars who hold the rebellion thesis is best described as:
o: skeptical, suggesting their view reflects modern taste more than evidence
Correct: paragraph 2 says the thesis flatters our own tastes and fits the evidence poorly.
admiring, since they first noticed the marginal images
Paragraph 2 criticizes the thesis rather than praising its holders.
contemptuous, dismissing any reading of medieval humor
Paragraph 4 accepts that the images could amuse, so dismissing humor is too extreme.
neutral, presenting their view without evaluating it
Paragraph 2 openly argues that the evidence fits the thesis poorly.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 says the rebellion thesis is appealing because it flatters our own tastes and that the evidence fits it poorly. That is reasoned skepticism. Contemptuous is too extreme: the author calls the thesis appealing and in paragraph 4 accepts that illuminators sometimes laughed, so the author does not dismiss medieval humor.

passages.title: The Grammar of Hearsay
text: In a number of the world's languages, including Turkish, Quechua, and Tuyuca, a speaker cannot simply say that it rained last night. The grammar demands that the sentence also mark how the speaker knows: whether she saw the rain, inferred it from wet streets, or was told about it by someone else. Linguists call this feature evidentiality, and it has attracted a good deal of romantic speculation. Surely, the thinking goes, speakers of such languages must be more scrupulous about truth, more careful to distinguish knowledge from rumor, than those of us who can assert anything without citing our sources.

The speculation is understandable but, I think, mistaken in an instructive way. Obligatory marking does not make speakers more honest; it makes a certain kind of information routine. When every sentence must carry an evidential, choosing one becomes as automatic as choosing a verb tense in English, and automatic choices are not moral achievements. A speaker can mark a claim as directly witnessed while lying about it, just as an English speaker can use the past tense to describe events that never happened. The grammar specifies what must be said, not whether what is said is true.

Nor is it clear that languages without grammatical evidentials leave speakers unable to track sources. English speakers have an abundant toolkit: apparently, I hear that, they say, I saw it with my own eyes. The difference is that in English such expressions are optional, and their presence is therefore noticeable. Paradoxically, this may give them more rhetorical force than their grammatical counterparts. When an English speaker goes out of her way to say she saw something herself, listeners take note precisely because she did not have to.

What evidential systems do reveal is that languages differ in which distinctions they make compulsory, and compulsory distinctions shape what speakers attend to in the moment of speaking. That is an interesting claim about habit and attention. It is not a claim about virtue, and conflating the two tells us more about our wish to find moral lessons in grammar than about grammar itself.

qs.q: Which statement best captures the author's central claim?
o: Languages with evidentials produce more honest speakers than other languages.
Paragraph 2 calls this romantic speculation mistaken.
English speakers cannot express how they know what they report.
Paragraph 3 lists many English expressions for doing exactly that.
Obligatory evidential marking shapes attention but does not make speakers more truthful.
Correct: paragraph 2 denies the honesty claim and paragraph 4 limits the effect to habit and attention.
Grammar has no effect at all on what speakers notice.
Paragraph 4 says compulsory distinctions do shape what speakers attend to.
qs.x: The author rejects the romantic idea that evidentials make speakers more honest (paragraph 2). Paragraph 4 then says that compulsory distinctions shape what speakers attend to. So the central claim has two parts: an effect on attention, but none on truthfulness. Saying grammar has no effect at all is too strong, because paragraph 4 grants the effect on attention.

qs.q: The comparison between evidentials and English verb tense in paragraph 2 is used to show that:
o: evidentials and tense are learned at the same age
Paragraph 2 says nothing about acquisition age.
English tense is a hidden form of evidentiality
Paragraph 2 treats tense as an analogy, not as an evidential system.
a grammatical requirement does not guarantee that the content is true
Correct: paragraph 2 notes one can use the past tense for events that never happened, and likewise lie with an evidential.
speakers choose tenses more carefully than evidentials
Paragraph 2 says both choices become equally automatic.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 notes that English speakers can use the past tense for events that never happened, just as one can mark a lie as witnessed. A grammatical requirement fixes the form of a sentence, not whether it is true. The analogy does not say English tense is a kind of evidential, and paragraph 2 says both choices are equally automatic.

qs.q: According to the passage, optional source expressions in English may:
o: carry extra rhetorical force because speakers did not have to use them
Correct: paragraph 3 says listeners take note precisely because the speaker did not have to.
be ignored by listeners because they are so common
Paragraph 3 says their presence is noticeable, not ignored.
be grammatically required in formal speech
Paragraph 3 calls these expressions optional in English.
convey less information than grammatical evidentials
Paragraph 3 suggests they may be more forceful, not less informative.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 says optional English expressions like 'I saw it with my own eyes' get noticed precisely because the speaker did not have to use them. This may give them more rhetorical force than grammatical evidentials. The tempting idea that common expressions get ignored contradicts the text, which says their presence is noticeable.

qs.q: Based on the passage, the author would expect a Quechua speaker who wanted to deceive a listener to:
o: be prevented by the grammar from stating the falsehood
Paragraph 2 says grammar specifies what must be said, not whether it is true.
be forced to use a hearsay marker for any false claim
No rule in paragraph 2 ties falsehood to the hearsay marker.
be detected automatically by native listeners
The passage never claims evidentials expose lies to listeners.
be able to mark a false claim as directly witnessed
Correct: paragraph 2 says a speaker can mark a claim as witnessed while lying about it.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 says a speaker can mark a claim as directly witnessed while lying about it, because grammar specifies what must be said, not whether it is true. So a deceptive Quechua speaker could simply use the witness marker. Nothing in the passage says the grammar prevents lies or that listeners can automatically detect them.

qs.q: Which finding would most challenge the author's position?
o: Children acquire evidential markers later than basic verb tenses.
Acquisition timing does not bear on paragraph 2's claim about honesty.
In controlled deception tasks, speakers of evidential languages lie far less often than matched speakers of other languages.
Correct: this ties evidential grammar to honesty, the link paragraphs 2 and 4 deny.
English speakers use expressions like 'apparently' very frequently.
Frequency of English source expressions does not test the honesty claim.
Speakers of evidential languages sometimes lie using the witness marker.
This supports paragraph 2, which says exactly this can happen.
qs.x: The author denies that evidential grammar makes speakers more honest (paragraphs 2 and 4). A controlled study showing that speakers of evidential languages lie far less than matched speakers would support the very link the author rejects. Lying with the witness marker is the case paragraph 2 describes, so that finding would support the author, not challenge the view.

qs.q: The claim in paragraph 2 that 'automatic choices are not moral achievements' depends on which assumption?
o: Most speakers of evidential languages are dishonest.
Paragraph 2 makes no claim that speakers are dishonest, only not more honest.
Moral credit requires something like deliberate effort rather than habitual compliance.
Correct: paragraph 2 denies credit to evidential choices precisely because they are routine, which presumes credit needs deliberation.
English has a complete grammatical evidential system.
Paragraph 3 says English expressions are optional, not grammatical evidentials.
Habitual behaviors cannot affect what speakers attend to.
Paragraph 4 says compulsory habits do shape attention.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 says evidential choices are not moral achievements because they are automatic. That reasoning works only if moral credit needs something like deliberate effort, not habit. The assumption is not that speakers are dishonest; the author says only that they are not more honest. Paragraph 4 also says habit does shape attention.

passages.title: Promises to the Dead
text: Suppose you promise a dying friend that you will scatter her ashes on a particular mountain, and after her death you find the trip expensive and inconvenient. Do you still owe her the journey? Most people feel strongly that you do. Yet it is surprisingly hard to say why. On the most common accounts of promising, obligations exist because the person to whom we promise has an interest in our keeping our word and can be wronged if we do not. The dead, it seems, have no interests, cannot be disappointed, and cannot be wronged. If so, the obligation should evaporate at the moment of death.

One response is to relocate the obligation to the living. Breaking deathbed promises, the argument runs, erodes a practice on which all of us depend; if such promises were routinely ignored, the dying would lose a source of comfort. This explanation is not wrong, but it gets the moral feel of the case backward. When I keep my promise to my friend, I do not think I am doing a favor for future dying people in general. I think I am doing something for her.

A more promising approach holds that some interests survive the person who had them. My friend cared, while alive, about what would happen to her remains, and that concern was directed at a time after her death. It is not strange to say that her interest is set back if her wishes are ignored, any more than it is strange to say that an author is wronged when her unfinished book is published under someone else's name after she dies. Harm, on this view, does not require that the victim experience it.

Critics object that this makes the dead into ghostly creditors whose claims could pile up forever. The worry deserves an answer, but not a retreat. Posthumous interests, like the claims of the living, can be weighed against other considerations, and they may fade as the people and projects they concern pass out of the world. Granting that the dead can be wronged does not require us to obey them without limit. It requires only that we stop pretending our sense of obligation is an illusion.

qs.q: The author's main position is that:
o: promises to the dead lapse at the moment of death
Paragraph 1 presents this as a puzzle the author goes on to reject.
deathbed promises matter only because they comfort the living
Paragraph 2 says this explanation gets the moral feel of the case backward.
the wishes of the dead must be obeyed without limit
Paragraph 4 explicitly says we need not obey the dead without limit.
the dead can have surviving interests that ground real but limited obligations
Correct: paragraph 3 defends surviving interests and paragraph 4 says they can be weighed and may fade.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 defends the idea that some interests survive the person who had them, and paragraph 4 adds that these interests can be weighed against others and may fade. Together they ground real but limited obligations. The view that promises lapse at death is the puzzle in paragraph 1, and paragraph 4 explicitly rejects obeying the dead without limit.

qs.q: The author's objection to relocating the obligation to the living is that this view:
o: misdescribes whom the promise-keeper takes herself to be acting for
Correct: paragraph 2 says the keeper acts for her friend, not for future dying people.
is factually wrong about the value of the promising practice
Paragraph 2 says the explanation is 'not wrong' about the practice.
would require keeping every promise regardless of cost
Paragraph 2 raises no objection about cost.
treats the dead as creditors with unlimited claims
That is the critics' worry about the author's own view in paragraph 4.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 grants that the living-practice explanation is 'not wrong' but says it gets the moral feel backward: the promise-keeper acts for her friend, not for future dying people in general. So the objection is about whom the act is for, not about facts. The ghostly-creditor worry belongs to critics of the author's own view in paragraph 4.

qs.q: The example of an unfinished book published under someone else's name functions in paragraph 3 to:
o: show that authors deserve stronger legal protection
Paragraph 3 makes a moral point, not a legal one.
illustrate how posthumous interests fade over time
Fading is discussed in paragraph 4, not illustrated by the book.
support the claim that a person can be harmed without experiencing it
Correct: paragraph 3 uses it to show we already accept posthumous wrongs.
argue that only artistic projects create lasting interests
Paragraph 3 pairs the book with the ashes case, so interests are not limited to art.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 argues that harm does not require that the victim experience it. Most readers already accept that a dead author is wronged when her book is published under someone else's name, so the example extends that intuition to the ashes case. Fading interests come up only in paragraph 4, and the example is about a moral wrong, not law.

qs.q: Which case would the author's view most clearly treat as wronging the deceased?
o: An heir sells a house the deceased never expressed any view about.
Without any concern directed past death, paragraph 3's mechanism has nothing to set back.
A town renames a street three centuries after its founder died silent on the matter.
No expressed interest exists, and paragraph 4 says interests fade with time.
A historian publishes a scholar's diaries that the scholar, while alive, explicitly asked to have destroyed.
Correct: an explicit wish aimed past death is set back, as in paragraph 3, even if no living person objects.
A family declines to follow a dead relative's request that is illegal to carry out.
Paragraph 4 allows posthumous interests to be outweighed, so this is not clearly a wrong.
qs.x: On the author's view a person is wronged when a concern she held while alive, aimed at a time after her death, is set back (paragraph 3). The scholar who explicitly asked that her diaries be destroyed fits this exactly. The illegal request is tempting, but paragraph 4 lets posthumous interests be outweighed, so refusing it is not clearly a wrong.

qs.q: How would the author most likely answer the critic who says honoring the dead would let their claims pile up forever?
o: Posthumous interests can be weighed against other concerns and may fade over time.
Correct: paragraph 4 gives exactly this answer.
The dead have no interests, so no claims can accumulate.
This is the view from paragraph 1 that the author rejects.
Only promises made on a deathbed create posthumous interests.
Paragraph 3 grounds interests in the person's concern, not the deathbed setting.
The living should defer to the dead whenever they conflict.
Paragraph 4 rejects obeying the dead without limit.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 takes up the ghostly-creditor objection directly. Posthumous interests, like those of the living, can be weighed against other concerns and may fade as the people and projects they concern pass away. Saying the dead have no interests is the paragraph 1 view the author rejects, so it could not be the author's reply.

passages.title: In Defense of the Vestibule
text: Modern residential design has been at war with the in-between. Open-plan living erased the hallway, the parlor, and the pantry in the name of light and flow, and the vestibule, that small chamber between the front door and the house proper, has nearly vanished from new construction. Architects who remove it are not careless; they see wasted square footage, a dark box that serves no function except to be passed through. In a market that prices homes by area, a room designed for passing through looks like an indulgence.

But the vestibule's function was never primarily spatial. In colder climates it served as an airlock, keeping winter out of the main rooms, and that practical role is real. Its deeper work, however, was social. A vestibule allowed a household to receive a visitor without fully admitting them, to sign for a parcel, decline a salesman, or greet a neighbor while keeping the life of the house out of view. It staged the passage from public to private as a sequence rather than a single step, and in doing so gave both host and guest a moment to adjust their manners.

When the front door opens directly onto the living room, that sequence collapses. Every arrival becomes an intrusion or a full admission; there is no intermediate state. Residents compensate in other ways, with doorbell cameras, with conversations conducted through a half-opened door, with a reluctance to answer at all. These improvisations suggest that the need the vestibule served did not disappear when the room did. It was merely left to be met badly.

I am not arguing that every house needs a small dark room by its front door, nor that older homes were socially superior. Many were built around rigid hierarchies of class and gender that no one should wish to restore. My point is narrower. Architecture encodes assumptions about how people meet, and when we judge rooms only by how much they hold, we lose sight of what they do. Some of the most useful spaces in a building are the ones in which nothing seems to happen.

qs.q: According to the passage, architects remove vestibules mainly because they regard them as:
o: relics of rigid class and gender hierarchies
Paragraph 4 raises hierarchies as the author's own concession, not architects' reason.
ineffective at keeping cold air out of the house
Paragraph 2 says the airlock role is real.
unpopular with visitors who dislike waiting
The passage never mentions visitors' dislike as architects' reason.
wasted area whose only function is to be passed through
Correct: paragraph 1 says architects see wasted square footage that serves only for passage.
qs.x: Paragraph 1 says architects see the vestibule as wasted square footage, a dark box whose only function is to be passed through. The hierarchy point is tempting, but it is the author's own concession in paragraph 4, not the architects' reason. Paragraph 2 says the airlock role is real, so architects do not reject the vestibule for failing to keep out cold.

qs.q: The author mentions doorbell cameras and conversations through a half-opened door in order to:
o: praise technology for replacing outdated rooms
Paragraph 3 calls these improvisations a bad way of meeting the need.
show that the social need the vestibule met persists and is met with poor substitutes
Correct: paragraph 3 says the need did not disappear but is now met badly.
argue that residents have become less friendly than before
Paragraph 3 attributes the behavior to design, not to a change in character.
prove that vestibules improved home security
Paragraph 2 frames the vestibule's role as social, not as security.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 says that without a vestibule, residents make do with doorbell cameras, half-opened doors, or not answering at all, and concludes that the need did not disappear but is now met badly. The examples are evidence that the social need persists. They are not praise for technology, and the author blames design, not a change in residents' character.

qs.q: Which function of the vestibule does the author consider most important?
o: Keeping winter air out of the main rooms
Paragraph 2 calls the airlock role real but secondary.
Staging the passage from public to private as a social sequence
Correct: paragraph 2 calls this its deeper work, beyond the spatial role.
Providing extra storage near the front door
Storage is never mentioned as a vestibule function.
Increasing a home's market value by area
Paragraph 1 says pricing by area is why vestibules look wasteful.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 says the airlock role is real but calls the vestibule's deeper work social: staging the passage from public to private as a sequence. The question asks what the author ranks highest, so the word 'deeper' decides it. Keeping out winter air is a true function in the passage, but the author treats it as secondary.

qs.q: The concession at the start of paragraph 4 serves primarily to:
o: admit that the argument of paragraph 3 was mistaken
Paragraph 4 keeps paragraph 3's argument while limiting its scope.
argue that open-plan homes are socially superior
Paragraph 4 only denies that older homes were superior; paragraph 3 says open plans meet the social need badly.
recommend a vestibule in every new house
Paragraph 4 explicitly says not every house needs one.
narrow the claim so it is not read as nostalgia for older social arrangements
Correct: paragraph 4 rejects restoring old hierarchies and says the point is narrower.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 opens by saying that not every house needs a vestibule and that older homes were not socially superior, since many reflected rigid class and gender hierarchies. This narrows the claim so it is not read as nostalgia. It does not take back paragraph 3's argument, and it does not suggest a vestibule in every house.

qs.q: Which design would the author most likely praise?
o: A deep, sheltered entry alcove where residents can talk with callers before inviting them in
Correct: it restores the intermediate state between public and private described in paragraph 2.
An entry converted into a closet to maximize storage space
This judges space by what it holds, the habit paragraph 4 criticizes.
A front door opening straight into the kitchen for efficiency
Paragraph 3 says direct entry collapses the social sequence.
A glass-walled facade that makes the interior fully visible
Paragraph 2 values keeping the life of the house out of view.
qs.x: The author values a space that lets residents receive callers without fully admitting them, an in-between state between public and private (paragraph 2). A deep entry alcove where residents can talk with callers before inviting them in restores that. Turning the entry into a closet judges space by what it holds, the habit paragraph 4 criticizes.

qs.q: Which finding would most undermine the author's claim in paragraph 3?
o: Doorbell cameras are more common in homes without vestibules.
This fits paragraph 3's claim that residents compensate with such devices.
Vestibules reduce winter heating costs in cold climates.
This concerns the airlock role from paragraph 2, not the social claim.
Residents of homes with and without vestibules answer the door equally often and feel equally at ease with callers.
Correct: paragraph 3 claims the need persists and is met badly; equal ease suggests no unmet need.
Many old homes with vestibules reflected class hierarchies.
Paragraph 4 already concedes this point.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 claims the social need the vestibule met still exists and is now met badly. If people in homes with and without vestibules answered the door equally often and felt equally at ease, there would be no sign of an unmet need. More doorbell cameras in homes without vestibules would support the claim, not weaken it.

passages.title: The Price of a Fair Temperament
text: Every piano tuned today is tuned slightly out of tune, and deliberately so. In equal temperament, the system that now governs nearly all Western keyboard music, the octave is divided into twelve identical semitones. The result is that no interval except the octave is acoustically pure. The major third, in particular, is noticeably wider than the simple ratio our ears find most consonant. In exchange for this universal small impurity, a keyboard can play in every key equally well, and a composer can modulate anywhere without fear.

The usual story presents this as plain progress: earlier tuning systems were awkward compromises that made remote keys unusable, and equal temperament liberated music from them. But the earlier systems were not simply defective. The many unequal temperaments used in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries made some keys sweeter and others harsher, and musicians of the time described keys as having distinct characters, one bright, another mournful, another restless. Composers chose keys partly for these colors. Under equal temperament, those distinctions shrank to nearly nothing, because every key is now an exact transposition of every other.

Why, then, did equal temperament prevail? Its advantages for modulation were real, but so were less elevated forces. Pianos were becoming mass-produced commodities, sold to households that could not afford a skilled tuner with opinions about temperament. A single, standardized system was easier to teach, to manufacture for, and to maintain. The triumph of equal temperament was in part a triumph of interchangeability, the same logic that standardized screws and railway gauges.

To say this is not to call for the abolition of the modern piano. Equal temperament made possible much music that I would not wish away. But we should recognize that it was a trade, not a discovery, and that something audible was given up. Performers who experiment with older tunings are sometimes dismissed as antiquarians. They might better be understood as recovering a dimension of musical meaning that convenience, more than art, persuaded us to forget.

qs.q: According to the passage, the chief musical advantage of equal temperament is that it:
o: makes every interval acoustically pure
Paragraph 1 says no interval except the octave is pure.
gives each key a distinct emotional character
Paragraph 2 says key characters shrank to nearly nothing under equal temperament.
lets every key be played equally well, allowing free modulation
Correct: paragraph 1 says a keyboard can play in every key and modulate anywhere.
makes the major third narrower and sweeter
Paragraph 1 says the equal-tempered third is wider than the pure ratio.
qs.x: Paragraph 1 says equal temperament accepts a small impurity in every interval except the octave so that a keyboard can play in every key equally well and modulate freely. That is the advantage. Distinct key characters are tempting, but paragraph 2 says they belonged to the older unequal systems and shrank to nearly nothing under equal temperament.

qs.q: The comparison to screws and railway gauges serves to suggest that equal temperament:
o: spread partly because of industrial pressures toward standardization
Correct: paragraph 3 calls its triumph partly a triumph of interchangeability.
was invented by engineers rather than musicians
Paragraph 3 compares the logic of adoption, not the identity of inventors.
is acoustically as precise as machined parts
Paragraph 1 stresses that equal temperament is deliberately impure.
was adopted only after it proved artistically superior
Paragraph 3 says less elevated forces than art drove its success.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 says the triumph of equal temperament was partly a triumph of interchangeability, and links it to mass-produced pianos and households that could not afford skilled tuners. The screws and gauges show that industrial standardization, not only art, drove its spread. The comparison is about why it was adopted, not who invented it.

qs.q: The passage indicates that the distinct characters of keys under unequal temperaments arose because:
o: composers assigned moods to keys by convention alone
Paragraph 2 ties the characters to audible tuning differences, not mere convention.
every key was an exact transposition of every other
Paragraph 2 says that is true of equal temperament, which erased the characters.
instruments of the period could not play remote keys
Paragraph 2 rejects the idea that earlier systems were simply defective.
the tuning of intervals differed from one key to another
Correct: paragraph 2 says unequal systems made some keys sweeter and others harsher.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 says unequal temperaments made some keys sweeter and others harsher. The characters came from real differences in how intervals were tuned from key to key. The exact-transposition answer describes equal temperament, the system that erased those characters, and the passage ties the moods to audible tuning, not to convention alone.

qs.q: Which evidence would most support the author's explanation of why equal temperament prevailed?
o: Treatises praising equal temperament for its pure major thirds
Paragraph 1 says its thirds are impure, so such praise would be mistaken and irrelevant.
Nineteenth-century piano makers' letters favoring it chiefly because it simplified factory tuning and repairs
Correct: this matches paragraph 3's claim that manufacturing and maintenance drove adoption.
Records showing professional tuners preferred unequal systems
This concerns tuners' tastes, not why the standard system spread to households.
Concerts in which audiences could not hear any tuning differences
This would undercut paragraph 4's claim that something audible was lost.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 explains the spread of equal temperament partly through mass production: one standard system was easier to teach, manufacture for, and maintain. Piano makers' letters favoring it because it simplified factory tuning and repairs would directly support that. Praise for pure thirds is tempting but conflicts with paragraph 1, which says the thirds are impure.

qs.q: The author's attitude toward performers who experiment with older tunings is best described as:
o: dismissive, regarding them as mere antiquarians
Paragraph 4 reports this dismissal by others and rejects it.
sympathetic, seeing them as recovering a lost dimension of meaning
Correct: paragraph 4 says they might better be understood as recovering musical meaning.
hostile, since they threaten the modern piano
Paragraph 4 says the author is not calling for the piano's abolition.
indifferent, treating the matter as purely technical
Paragraph 4 argues that something audible and meaningful is at stake.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 says these performers are sometimes dismissed as antiquarians but might better be seen as recovering a dimension of musical meaning that convenience made us forget. That is sympathy. The dismissive answer is the trap: it describes what others think, a view the author reports in order to reject it.

passages.title: Government by Lottery
text: Ask most people what makes a political system democratic and they will answer: elections. Yet for the Athenians who gave us the word, elections were an aristocratic device. Most Athenian magistrates were chosen by lot from among eligible citizens, and Aristotle could describe selection by lot as characteristic of democracy and election as characteristic of oligarchy. Election, the reasoning went, invites voters to pick the best, and the best in any society tend to be those with wealth, education, and reputation already.

Modern democracies have inherited the electoral half of this legacy and forgotten the other. The consequences are familiar. Legislatures drawn by election are dramatically wealthier, older, and more professionally homogeneous than the populations they govern. Campaigns reward fundraising, and the skills that win campaigns are not obviously the skills that make good laws. None of this is a scandal or a conspiracy; it is simply what elections, as a selection mechanism, tend to produce.

Lottery offers a different promise. A randomly selected assembly of sufficient size would resemble the public statistically, in income, occupation, region, and outlook, without anyone having to engineer the result. Its members would owe nothing to donors and would have no reelection to pursue. Recent experiments with citizens' assemblies, in which randomly chosen residents deliberate over a contested question with access to experts, suggest that ordinary people can master complex material and reach considered judgments.

The obvious objection is competence: surely we want our laws written by people who know what they are doing. But this objection proves less than it seems. Elected legislators are not chosen for expertise either; they are chosen for electability, and they rely heavily on staff and specialists. A chamber chosen by lot could rely on the same support. I do not propose replacing elections wholesale. A legislature with one elected chamber and one chosen by lot would combine accountability with representativeness, and it would remind us that voting is only one of the ways a people can rule itself.

qs.q: According to the passage, Aristotle associated election with:
o: democracy
Paragraph 1 says Aristotle linked lot, not election, to democracy.
monarchy
Monarchy is never mentioned in paragraph 1.
tyranny
Tyranny is never mentioned in paragraph 1.
oligarchy
Correct: paragraph 1 says Aristotle described election as characteristic of oligarchy.
qs.x: Paragraph 1 says Aristotle described selection by lot as characteristic of democracy and election as characteristic of oligarchy. The reasoning was that election picks 'the best,' who tend to be the already wealthy and well known. Democracy is the trap, because modern readers link elections with democracy, the very assumption the passage questions.

qs.q: The author's main purpose is to argue that:
o: selection by lot deserves a place alongside elections in democratic institutions
Correct: paragraph 4 proposes one elected chamber and one chosen by lot.
elections should be abolished in favor of lotteries
Paragraph 4 says the author does not propose replacing elections wholesale.
Athenian democracy was superior to modern democracy
The passage borrows an Athenian idea without ranking whole systems.
elected legislators are corrupt and serve donors
Paragraph 2 says the problem is not a scandal or a conspiracy.
qs.x: The argument builds to paragraph 4's proposal: one elected chamber and one chosen by lot, adding lottery alongside elections. The author explicitly says elections should not be replaced wholesale, so the abolition answer is too extreme. Paragraph 2 also denies that elected legislators are part of a scandal or conspiracy.

qs.q: In paragraph 2, the author presents the unrepresentativeness of elected legislatures as:
o: evidence of a deliberate conspiracy by elites
Paragraph 2 explicitly denies any conspiracy.
a temporary problem that campaign reform will fix
Paragraph 2 treats it as built into the mechanism, not temporary.
a predictable result of how elections select people
Correct: paragraph 2 says it is simply what elections as a mechanism tend to produce.
an unimportant side effect of voter apathy
Paragraph 2 never mentions apathy and treats the effect as significant.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 says the wealth and sameness of elected legislatures is not a scandal or a conspiracy but simply what elections, as a selection mechanism, tend to produce. A predictable result of the mechanism matches this. The conspiracy answer contradicts an explicit denial, and calling it temporary ignores that it is built into how elections work.

qs.q: Which finding would most weaken the author's reply to the competence objection?
o: Elected legislators rely heavily on specialist staff.
Paragraph 4 already states this as part of the reply.
Citizens' assemblies reached considered judgments on hard questions.
Paragraph 3 cites this as support for lottery.
With identical staff support, members chosen by lot are far more easily steered by advisers than elected legislators.
Correct: paragraph 4's reply rests on the claim that a lot-chosen chamber could use the same support just as well.
Campaign skills differ from the skills of good lawmaking.
Paragraph 2 makes this point in the author's favor.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 answers the competence objection by noting that elected members also rely on staff, so a chamber chosen by lot could use the same support. If lot-chosen members given identical support were far more easily steered by their advisers, that support would not work the same way, and the reply would fail. The other choices repeat the author's own supporting points.

qs.q: Which reform is most consistent with the author's proposal?
o: Adding a randomly selected chamber to review laws passed by an elected chamber
Correct: paragraph 4 proposes pairing an elected chamber with one chosen by lot.
Requiring all candidates for office to hold university degrees
This would deepen the elite skew criticized in paragraph 2.
Replacing every elected office with one filled by lottery
Paragraph 4 rejects replacing elections wholesale.
Extending legislative terms to reduce how often elections occur
This changes election timing, not the selection mechanism paragraph 3 favors.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 proposes a legislature with one elected chamber and one chosen by lot, combining accountability with representativeness. Adding a randomly selected review chamber beside an elected one fits this. Replacing every office with lottery is tempting but goes too far, since the author says elections should not be replaced wholesale.

qs.q: Which can most reasonably be inferred about Athenian practice from paragraph 1?
o: Athenians chose every public official by lot.
Paragraph 1 says most, not all, magistrates were chosen by lot.
Athenians used lot because it selected the most competent citizens.
Paragraph 1 links picking 'the best' to election, not lot.
Aristotle wished to abolish democracy in Athens.
Paragraph 1 reports Aristotle's classification, not any wish of his.
Athenians did not treat elections as the defining feature of democracy.
Correct: paragraph 1 says they saw elections as aristocratic and lot as democratic.
qs.x: Paragraph 1 says Athenians chose most magistrates by lot and treated election as aristocratic, so they did not see elections as the defining feature of democracy. Note the word 'most': it rules out the claim that every official was chosen by lot. The passage also links picking 'the best' to election, not to lot.

passages.title: The Moral Order of the Queue
text: Few institutions seem as humble as the queue. A line of strangers waiting for a bus or a ticket window appears to need no explanation: people arrive, and they are served in the order they arrived. Yet anthropologists who have watched queues in different places have found them to be anything but simple. A queue is a small society with its own law, enforced not by police but by glances, murmurs, and the occasional public rebuke, and the law differs from place to place.

In some settings, a person may hold a place for a friend who arrives later; in others, the practice is an outrage. In some, an object such as a bag or a stone can stand in line for its owner; in others, only bodies count. Some queues tolerate a frail elder moving to the front, while others insist that need is no excuse. Observers who treat one of these arrangements as the natural form of fairness and the others as disorder have mistaken a local custom for a universal principle.

What all these systems share is not a single rule but a single problem. Wherever more people want something than can have it at once, someone must decide who goes first, and the queue is one answer among several. Others include price, rank, lottery, and force. The queue's distinctive claim is that time spent waiting is a kind of payment that everyone can make, and its moral appeal lies in that apparent equality. But the equality is less complete than it looks. Waiting costs more for a worker paid by the hour than for a retiree, and services that let people pay to skip lines expose the fact that time was never equally priced.

This is why disputes about queue-jumping are heated out of all proportion to the minutes at stake. The person who cuts in line steals very little time. What she threatens is the shared fiction that, in this one small space, everyone is equal before the clock. People defend that fiction fiercely because, on reflection, they suspect how fragile it is.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses the main point of the passage?
o: Queues are the fairest possible way to allocate scarce goods.
Paragraph 3 says the queue's equality is less complete than it looks.
Queues are culturally variable moral orders resting on a fragile claim of equality.
Correct: paragraph 2 stresses variation and paragraphs 3-4 the fragile equality behind the queue.
All societies follow the same basic rules for waiting in line.
Paragraph 2 says the rules differ from place to place.
Queue-jumping is wrong mainly because it wastes others' time.
Paragraph 4 says the cutter steals very little time.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 shows that queue rules vary from place to place, and paragraphs 3 and 4 argue that the queue rests on a claim of equality that is incomplete and fragile. The main point joins both ideas. The fairest-system answer is tempting but conflicts with paragraph 3, which says the queue's equality is less complete than it looks.

qs.q: According to the passage, the rules of a queue are enforced mainly by:
o: police and other official authorities
Paragraph 1 says enforcement is not by police.
informal social pressure such as glances and rebukes
Correct: paragraph 1 says enforcement comes from glances, murmurs, and public rebukes.
written regulations posted at service points
Paragraph 1 never mentions written rules.
payments collected from those who wait
Paragraph 3 discusses paying to skip lines, not paying to enforce rules.
qs.x: Paragraph 1 says a queue's law is enforced not by police but by glances, murmurs, and the occasional public rebuke, which is informal social pressure. The payment answer borrows words from paragraph 3, which is about paying to skip lines, not about enforcing the rules of the line.

qs.q: The author supports the claim that the queue's equality 'is less complete than it looks' chiefly by noting that:
o: some queues let objects hold a place for their owners
That example in paragraph 2 illustrates cultural variation, not unequal costs.
queues are enforced without police
Paragraph 1's point about enforcement does not address equality of cost.
lottery and force are alternatives to the queue
Paragraph 3 lists alternatives but does not use them to show inequality.
waiting imposes different costs on people in different economic situations
Correct: paragraph 3 contrasts the hourly worker with the retiree.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 backs the 'less complete' claim by noting that waiting costs an hourly worker more than a retiree, and that paid line-skipping shows time was never equally priced. The objects-in-line example is tempting because it is a real detail, but paragraph 2 uses it to show cultural variation, not unequal costs.

qs.q: A society in which people leave their shoes in line to reserve places would, according to the passage, best be seen as:
o: one local custom among many rather than a form of disorder
Correct: paragraph 2 warns against treating one arrangement as natural and others as disorder.
evidence that its queues have broken down
Paragraph 2 calls this kind of judgment a mistake.
proof that objects should never stand in for people
Paragraph 2 notes that some places accept objects in line.
an example of allocation by force rather than waiting
Leaving shoes is still a waiting system, not force as in paragraph 3.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 lists objects holding places as an accepted custom in some settings and warns against treating one arrangement as natural and the others as disorder. So the shoe practice is one local custom among many. Calling it a breakdown is the very mistake paragraph 2 criticizes, and leaving shoes is still waiting, not force.

qs.q: Which observation would most support the author's explanation of anger at queue-jumpers?
o: Anger at a cutter rises in direct proportion to the minutes others lose.
This ties the anger to time, which paragraph 4 says is not the real stake.
Most people in long lines never notice when someone cuts in.
If cutting went unnoticed, it would not explain paragraph 4's heated disputes.
People react just as angrily to someone cutting one place ahead as to someone cutting twenty places.
Correct: anger unrelated to time lost fits paragraph 4's claim that the offense is to equality, not minutes.
Queues that allow place-holding see more disputes than others.
This concerns local rules from paragraph 2, not the source of anger.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 says queue-jumping disputes are heated out of all proportion to the minutes at stake, because the cutter threatens a shared fiction of equality, not people's time. Anger that is the same whether someone cuts one place or twenty fits this best. Anger that grows with minutes lost would point to time as the real issue, the opposite of the author's view.

passages.title: Written by the Installment
text: Many of the most celebrated English novels of the nineteenth century were not first read as books at all. They appeared in monthly or weekly parts, a few chapters at a time, over a year or more, and readers lived with them the way we now live with television series, waiting, speculating, and arguing between installments. Literary criticism has long treated this mode of publication as a commercial accident, an external circumstance to be set aside when we turn to the finished work bound between covers.

That approach misses how deeply the installment shaped the form. A writer publishing in parts could not revise early chapters in light of later developments; what had been printed was fixed. Each part needed its own small arc and, ideally, an ending that would send readers back to the bookseller next month. The famously sprawling casts of these novels, with their subplots weaving in and out, served a practical purpose: a large company of characters allowed an author to rest one storyline while advancing another, and to keep readers who disliked one thread loyal to the rest.

Serialization also made the novel unusually responsive to its audience. Authors read reviews and letters as the work appeared, and there are well-documented cases in which a minor character who proved popular was given more space, or a plot was bent to meet the public's appetite. Critics who prize the autonomy of the artist have sometimes seen this as a corruption. I would call it a collaboration, conducted in public and at a pace no later form of literature matched until quite recently.

Reading these novels in a single volume, as students now do, is not illegitimate, but it changes them. The cliffhangers flatten into chapter breaks, the long digressions that once filled a reader's month become obstacles to be skimmed, and the sense of a story unfolding alongside one's own life disappears. If we want to understand why these books took the shapes they did, we should at least try to imagine them as they were first encountered: incomplete, uncertain, and shared.

qs.q: According to the passage, an author publishing a novel in installments could NOT:
o: respond to readers' letters during publication
Paragraph 3 says authors did read and respond to letters.
end a part in a way that encouraged further buying
Paragraph 2 says each part ideally ended this way.
revise early chapters after they had been printed
Correct: paragraph 2 says what had been printed was fixed.
expand the role of a popular minor character
Paragraph 3 describes cases in which exactly this happened.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 says a serial author could not revise early chapters in light of later ones, because what had been printed was fixed. The other three choices are things the passage says serial authors did do: answer readers, end parts with hooks, and expand popular characters. In NOT questions, rule out each choice the text confirms.

qs.q: The author suggests that the large casts of serialized novels were useful because they:
o: let authors alternate storylines and keep readers loyal
Correct: paragraph 2 says many characters let authors rest one thread and retain readers.
made each novel easier to bind as a single volume
Paragraph 2 ties large casts to serial needs, not to binding.
reflected the crowded cities in which readers lived
Urban life is never mentioned as a reason in paragraph 2.
allowed authors to revise earlier chapters freely
Paragraph 2 says revision of printed parts was impossible.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 says a large cast let an author rest one storyline while advancing another and keep readers who disliked one thread loyal to the rest. That is a practical serial reason. The revision answer contradicts paragraph 2, which says printed parts were fixed, and binding into one volume is not why the casts were large.

qs.q: The author's view of audience influence on serialized novels is best described as:
o: critical, treating it as a corruption of artistic autonomy
Paragraph 3 attributes this view to other critics, not the author.
dismissive, regarding it as too rare to matter
Paragraph 3 calls the cases well documented.
resigned, accepting it as a commercial necessity
Paragraph 3 praises it rather than merely tolerating it.
approving, treating it as a form of public collaboration
Correct: paragraph 3 says the author would call it a collaboration.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 says some critics see audience influence as a corruption, but the author would call it a collaboration, conducted in public. That is approval. The critical answer is the trap, because it is the view of other critics that the author describes and then rejects.

qs.q: Which modern situation is most analogous to the serial novel as the passage describes it?
o: A novelist who finishes a book in secret and releases it all at once
This lacks the installments and audience feedback that paragraphs 2-3 describe.
A web-comic artist who posts weekly, reads comments, and expands a side character readers love
Correct: it matches paragraph 3's audience responsiveness and paragraph 2's part-by-part release.
A film studio that remasters a classic movie for a new release
Remastering an existing work involves no unfolding, responsive composition.
A poet who revises old poems for a collected edition
Paragraph 2 stresses that serial authors could not revise published parts.
qs.x: The passage stresses two features: release in parts over time (paragraph 2) and responsiveness to readers while the work is still appearing (paragraph 3). A web comic posted weekly whose artist reads comments and expands a beloved side character has both. A book released all at once lacks both, and revising old poems clashes with paragraph 2's point that printed parts were fixed.

qs.q: Which discovery would most challenge the author's account in paragraph 2?
o: Readers wrote letters complaining about a dull subplot.
This fits paragraph 2's point about keeping readers who disliked one thread.
A leading serial novelist had completed every chapter, subplots included, before the first part appeared.
Correct: this suggests the form was not shaped by part-by-part composition as paragraph 2 claims.
Some installments ended on dramatic cliffhangers.
Paragraph 2 says parts ideally ended this way.
Modern students skim the long digressions in these novels.
Paragraph 4 already predicts this.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 argues that installment publication shaped the form: unrevisable parts, arcs for each part, and casts big enough to rotate storylines. If a leading serial novelist had finished every chapter before the first part appeared, the form would not have come from part-by-part writing. Letters about a dull subplot fit the author's point about loyal readers.

qs.q: The author claims that reading serialized novels in a single volume:
o: should be replaced entirely by reading in installments
Paragraph 4 asks only that we try to imagine the original experience.
leaves the reader's experience essentially unchanged
Paragraph 4 lists several ways the experience changes.
reveals the novels' true structure more clearly
Paragraph 4 says single-volume reading obscures why the books took their shapes.
is legitimate but alters how the work affects readers
Correct: paragraph 4 says it is not illegitimate, but it changes them.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 says reading these novels in a single volume is not illegitimate but changes them: cliffhangers flatten, digressions become obstacles, and the shared unfolding is lost. The answer must keep both halves. The replace-entirely answer overshoots, since the author asks only that we try to imagine the first readers' experience.

passages.title: Notches of Credit
text: Textbooks often tell the origin of money as a story about barter. Imagine, they say, a farmer with grain who wants shoes from a cobbler who does not want grain; to escape this awkward mismatch, people settled on some commodity everyone would accept, and coins followed. The story is tidy, and it has the appeal of logic. Its weakness is that historians and anthropologists have had great difficulty finding any society in which barter between neighbors was the ordinary way of exchanging goods.

What they have found instead, again and again, is credit. Neighbors who traded with one another kept running accounts, settled periodically or simply carried for years. Medieval England offers a vivid example in the tally stick, a piece of wood notched to record a debt and then split lengthwise so that creditor and debtor each kept a half. Because the notches ran across both pieces, neither party could alter the record without the alteration showing when the halves were matched. For centuries the royal treasury used tallies to record payments and obligations, and tallies could themselves change hands, so that a claim on a debtor became something one could pass to a third party.

If credit came first, then money is better understood as a social relationship than as a thing. A coin, on this view, is not valuable because of the metal in it but because it is accepted in settlement of obligations, above all the obligation to pay taxes. The state that demands taxes in a particular token creates demand for that token. The metal is a convenience and, perhaps, a reassurance, but not the source of value.

The barter story is not harmless. By imagining money as a neutral tool invented to smooth trade among equals, it hides the role of debt, power, and political authority in shaping economic life. I do not claim that the credit account settles every question about money. But a history that begins with the tally rather than the imagined cobbler would at least start with what people actually did.

qs.q: According to the passage, the main weakness of the barter story is that:
o: few if any societies are known where barter among neighbors was the usual mode of exchange
Correct: paragraph 1 says scholars have had great difficulty finding such a society.
it fails to explain why coins were made of metal
Paragraph 1 identifies a lack of evidence, not this gap, as its weakness.
it is too complicated to teach in textbooks
Paragraph 1 calls the story tidy and logical.
it overstates how often farmers needed shoes
Paragraph 1 uses the cobbler only as the textbook illustration.
qs.x: Paragraph 1 says the barter story's weakness is that historians and anthropologists have had great difficulty finding any society where barter between neighbors was the ordinary way to exchange goods. So the weakness is a lack of evidence, not a flaw in logic. The story is even called tidy and logical, which rules out the too-complicated answer.

qs.q: Splitting a tally stick lengthwise served mainly to:
o: make the debt easier to divide among several creditors
Paragraph 2 describes one creditor and one debtor each keeping a half.
double the value of the debt recorded on the stick
Nothing in paragraph 2 suggests splitting changed the debt's value.
keep either party from altering the record without detection
Correct: paragraph 2 says any alteration would show when the halves were matched.
allow the treasury to mint coins from the wood
Paragraph 2 never links tallies to minting coins.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 says the notches ran across both halves, so neither party could change the record without the change showing when the halves were matched. Splitting made tampering detectable. The several-creditors answer is tempting but wrong: the text describes exactly two halves, one for the creditor and one for the debtor.

qs.q: The author's claim that money is 'a social relationship' rests most directly on the idea that:
o: metal coins are more durable than wooden tallies
Paragraph 3 calls metal a convenience, not the source of value.
barter was common between strangers but not neighbors
The passage never makes this distinction.
a coin's value comes from its acceptance in settling obligations such as taxes
Correct: paragraph 3 says a coin is valuable because it settles obligations, not because of its metal.
traders preferred coins because they were tidy and logical
Paragraph 1 applies 'tidy' to the barter story, not to coins.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 says that if credit came first, a coin is valuable not for its metal but because it is accepted in settling obligations, above all taxes. That acceptance is what makes money a social relationship rather than a thing. The point about metal durability misses this, since the author calls metal a convenience, not the source of value.

qs.q: Which observation would the view in paragraph 3 best explain?
o: A token with no intrinsic worth comes into wide use soon after a government requires taxes to be paid in it.
Correct: paragraph 3 says demanding taxes in a token creates demand for that token.
Gold coins keep their value after the issuing state collapses.
This suggests value from metal, which paragraph 3 downplays.
Neighbors in a village trade grain directly for shoes.
This is the barter picture paragraph 1 says is rarely found.
Coins trade at the value of their metal wherever they travel.
This treats metal as the source of value, which paragraph 3 denies.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 says a state that demands taxes in a particular token creates demand for that token, whatever its metal. A worthless token coming into wide use once taxes must be paid in it is exactly what that view predicts. Gold coins keeping their value after the state collapses would suggest that value comes from the metal, which the author denies.

qs.q: The author says the barter story 'is not harmless' because it:
o: encourages people to take on excessive personal debt
Paragraph 4 is about what the story hides, not about behavior it causes.
exaggerates the importance of the royal treasury
Paragraph 4 criticizes the barter story, which never mentions the treasury.
overstates the role of the state in creating money
The author argues the barter story understates, not overstates, the state's role.
conceals the role of debt, power, and political authority in economic life
Correct: paragraph 4 says it hides these by imagining money as a neutral tool.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 says the barter story pictures money as a neutral tool for trade among equals and so hides the role of debt, power, and political authority. The overstating answer reverses the point: the author thinks the barter story leaves the state out. The passage says nothing about the story encouraging personal debt.

qs.q: Which discovery would most weaken the author's argument?
o: Additional medieval tally sticks stored in treasury archives
More tallies would support the evidence in paragraph 2.
A well-documented society whose neighbors routinely traded goods by direct barter, with no credit records
Correct: this supplies the evidence paragraph 1 says scholars have struggled to find.
A village where neighbors carried running accounts for years
This matches the credit practices paragraph 2 describes.
A state that accepted only its own tokens for tax payments
This fits paragraph 3's tax-driven account of money.
qs.x: The author's case starts from paragraph 1's claim that no society is known where neighbors usually bartered. A well-documented society that routinely bartered directly, with no credit records, would supply the missing evidence and weaken the credit-first account. More tally sticks or running accounts would support the author, not weaken the argument.

passages.title: The Bedside and the Ledger
text: Histories of medicine like to stage a duel. On one side stands the old physician, who reads each patient as a singular case and trusts the trained intuition of his fingertips. On the other stands the statistician, who counts outcomes across hundreds of patients and lets the numbers speak. In the triumphal version of the story, the ledger wins, superstition retreats, and modern medicine is born. I think this version gets the winner right and the battle wrong.

Consider the Parisian physician Pierre Louis, who in the 1830s tallied the courses of pneumonia patients bled early or late and concluded that bloodletting did far less good than his colleagues believed. Louis is usually cast as the hero of the duel. Yet his opponents did not object to counting as such; many of them counted constantly, recording pulses, temperatures and fluid losses. What they resisted was the claim that an average drawn from many bodies could tell a physician what to do with the one body in front of him. That objection was not superstition. It was a serious question about how a general truth becomes a particular decision, and it has never been fully answered.

What the numerical method actually changed was not the amount of knowledge but its address. Before Louis, medical authority lived in the person of the experienced practitioner, who could not easily be contradicted by anyone who had not stood at the same bedsides. After him, authority increasingly lived in tables that anyone literate could inspect, dispute and extend. The ledger made medical knowledge portable, cumulative and public. That is a genuine achievement, but it is an achievement in the social organization of knowledge, not a victory of reason over unreason.

Seeing the change this way matters because the old question returns whenever we forget it. A clinician who applies a trial's average result to a frail ninety-year-old patient who resembles no one in the trial is facing exactly the difficulty Louis's critics raised. The honest response is neither to discard the ledger nor to worship it, but to admit that every application of a statistic to a person is an act of judgment, and to train that judgment as carefully as we once trained the fingertips.

qs.q: The author's central claim about the rise of the numerical method is that it primarily:
o: proved that clinical intuition had always been a form of superstition
Paragraph 2 explicitly denies that the critics' objection was superstition.
increased the total amount of reliable knowledge available to doctors
Paragraph 3 says it changed 'not the amount of knowledge but its address.'
relocated medical authority from individual practitioners to shared, inspectable records
Correct: paragraph 3 says the method changed the 'address' of knowledge, making it portable and public.
ended the use of bloodletting in Parisian hospitals within a decade
The passage reports Louis's conclusion but says nothing about how quickly practice changed.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 states the thesis directly: the numerical method changed 'not the amount of knowledge but its address,' moving authority from the practitioner's person into tables anyone could inspect. The tempting choice about increasing knowledge is the exact idea that sentence denies, and the superstition choice contradicts paragraph 2's defense of the critics.

qs.q: The author mentions that Louis's opponents 'counted constantly' (paragraph 2) most likely in order to:
o: show that the dispute was about applying averages, not about whether to count
Correct: paragraph 2 says what they resisted was using an average to decide about one body.
suggest that Louis copied his method from his own critics
The passage never says Louis borrowed the method from anyone.
demonstrate that the critics' data were more accurate than Louis's
No comparison of data accuracy is made anywhere in the passage.
argue that bloodletting was in fact an effective treatment
The author does not defend bloodletting; the point concerns reasoning from averages.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 notes the critics counted constantly to show that counting itself was never in dispute; what they resisted was letting an average from many bodies dictate treatment of one body. Watch for choices that read in claims the passage never makes, such as Louis borrowing his method or bloodletting actually working.

qs.q: Which phrase best captures the author's attitude toward the 'triumphal version' of medical history?
o: Complete endorsement of both its conclusion and its framing
