The author rejects the duel framing as misleading.
Complete rejection, since the old physicians were proved right
The author grants the ledger 'won' and calls it a genuine achievement.
Indifference, since historical narratives cannot affect practice
Paragraph 4 says the framing matters because the old question returns in practice.
Partial agreement with its conclusion but rejection of its framing
Correct: paragraph 1 says it 'gets the winner right and the battle wrong.'
qs.x: Paragraph 1 ends with the key line: the triumphal story 'gets the winner right and the battle wrong.' So the author accepts that the ledger won but rejects framing it as reason defeating superstition. Total rejection fails because paragraph 3 calls the method a genuine achievement.

qs.q: Which modern situation most closely parallels the difficulty raised by Louis's critics?
o: Debating whether hospital records should be stored electronically or on paper
Storage format does not involve applying a group average to an individual.
Deciding whether a drug tested only on young adults should be given to a child
Correct: like the frail patient in paragraph 4, the child resembles no one in the trial.
Determining whether a trial had enough participants to detect an effect
This concerns the trial's internal validity, not applying its result to one person.
Choosing which journal should publish a large epidemiological study
Publication venue is unrelated to the general-to-particular problem.
qs.x: The critics' problem in paragraph 2 is how a general truth from a group becomes a decision about one person, and paragraph 4 applies it to a frail elder unlike anyone in the trial. A child given a drug tested only on young adults is the same gap. Sample-size questions are tempting but concern whether the trial itself is valid, not how to apply its result.

qs.q: Suppose historians found that, after Louis, junior doctors began successfully challenging senior doctors by citing published tables. How would this affect the author's argument?
o: It would weaken the claim that the critics raised a serious question
Who won arguments does not show the critics' question about averages was frivolous.
It would support the claim that numbers shifted where authority resided
Correct: paragraph 3 argues tables let anyone literate dispute established practitioners.
It would weaken the claim that the ledger made knowledge cumulative
Citing published tables is an instance of knowledge being shared and built upon.
It would have no bearing, since the author discusses only Louis himself
The author makes broad claims about the social organization of medical knowledge.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 argues that after Louis, authority moved into public tables that 'anyone literate could inspect, dispute and extend.' Junior doctors winning arguments by citing tables is direct evidence for that shift. It does not weaken the critics' question, because who wins an argument says nothing about whether averages fit individual patients.

qs.q: Which assumption is necessary for the author's recommendation in the final paragraph?
o: Clinical trials systematically exclude elderly patients on purpose
The example needs only that some patients differ from trial populations, not deliberate exclusion.
Fingertip diagnosis was more accurate than statistical diagnosis
The author never ranks the accuracy of the two methods.
Most clinicians already worship statistical averages
The author warns against worship but does not assume most clinicians do it.
Judgment in applying statistics can be improved through deliberate training
Correct: the author urges us to 'train that judgment,' which presumes it is trainable.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 recommends that we 'train that judgment' in applying statistics, which only makes sense if such judgment can be improved by training. A necessary assumption is one the argument collapses without. The claim about deliberate exclusion of the elderly is tempting but goes too far: the example needs only that some patients differ from trial populations.

passages.title: The Laundromat Parliament
text: Debates about neighborhood change tend to fixate on the dramatic: the shuttered family restaurant, the rent that doubles, the long-time resident forced across town. These losses are real, and they deserve the attention they receive. But the most consequential casualties of a changing block are often places no one would think to mourn, because no one thought of them as places at all.

Take the laundromat. Nobody goes there to socialize; people go because they lack a washing machine at home. Yet that very compulsion is what makes it valuable. Every week the same people are obliged to wait in the same room for roughly the same forty minutes. Over months, nods become greetings, greetings become exchanges about a sick child or a landlord who will not fix the heat, and a web of acquaintance forms among people who would never have chosen one another. Sociologists call such links weak ties, and a long line of research suggests they matter more than their name implies: they carry news of jobs, apartments and services across the boundaries of family and close friendship.

What the laundromat offers, then, is not community in the warm sense that planners like to invoke, but something more modest and perhaps more durable: repeated, involuntary co-presence. The café that replaces it may be friendlier, better lit and full of conversation, but its patrons arrive by choice, often already in pairs, and leave when they please. Chosen sociability tends to sort people by taste and income. Obligatory sociability mixes them.

I do not mean to romanticize drudgery or argue that residents should be denied the convenience of in-unit appliances. The point is narrower. When we measure what a neighborhood has lost, we count the institutions that announce their social function and overlook those that perform it quietly. A city that wants to preserve the connective tissue of its poorer districts should look less at the landmarks residents name in surveys and more at the unglamorous rooms where they are forced, week after week, to wait together.

qs.q: According to the passage, the laundromat's social value arises mainly from the fact that:
o: its users must return regularly and wait together whether they wish to or not
Correct: paragraph 3 credits 'repeated, involuntary co-presence.'
it is designed by planners to foster community among neighbors
Paragraph 3 contrasts the laundromat with the 'warm' community planners invoke.
its customers usually arrive in pairs and stay as long as they like
Paragraph 3 attributes this pattern to café patrons, not laundromat users.
it offers better lighting and comfort than nearby cafés
Paragraph 3 says the café, not the laundromat, may be friendlier and better lit.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 names the source of value: 'repeated, involuntary co-presence,' meaning the same people must wait together every week whether they want to or not. The traps attach features of the café (arriving in pairs, better lighting) to the laundromat, or reverse paragraph 3's contrast with planners' warm community.

qs.q: The author's claim that 'obligatory sociability mixes' people (paragraph 3) rests most directly on which idea?
o: Weak ties are emotionally stronger than ties between close friends
Paragraph 2 says weak ties carry information, not that they are emotionally stronger.
Poorer residents are more sociable than wealthier residents
The passage makes no claim about differences in sociability by income.
People who choose where to socialize tend to sort themselves by taste and income
Correct: paragraph 3 states chosen sociability sorts people, so compulsion avoids that sorting.
Cafés deliberately exclude customers who cannot afford their prices
The author says chosen settings sort people, not that cafés exclude anyone on purpose.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 reasons by contrast: chosen sociability sorts people by taste and income, so sociability that is forced avoids that sorting and mixes them. The weak-ties choice is tempting because weak ties appear in paragraph 2, but the passage says they carry information, not that they are emotionally stronger.

qs.q: The final paragraph serves primarily to:
o: introduce new evidence that weak ties help residents find jobs
Job-finding is mentioned in paragraph 2; the final paragraph adds no new evidence.
concede that in-unit appliances have harmed poorer neighborhoods
The author explicitly declines to argue against in-unit appliances.
reject the view that losing family restaurants is a real harm
Paragraph 1 calls those losses real and deserving of attention.
limit the scope of the argument and draw a practical implication
Correct: the author disclaims romanticizing drudgery, then urges attention to unglamorous rooms.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 opens by narrowing the claim (no romanticizing drudgery, no opposition to in-unit machines) and then draws a policy lesson: cities should look at unglamorous rooms where residents must wait together. Choice of conceding that appliances harmed neighborhoods misreads a disclaimer as an admission.

qs.q: Based on the passage, which setting would the author most likely regard as performing a similar quiet social function?
o: A members-only book club that meets monthly in a private home
Members choose to attend and share tastes, the sorting the author associates with chosen sociability.
A popular rooftop bar that attracts visitors from across the city
Its patrons arrive by choice and change constantly, so there is no repeated co-presence.
A bus stop where the same commuters wait each weekday morning
Correct: like the laundromat, it compels repeated waiting among the same people.
A neighborhood festival held once a year in the central square
A yearly event lacks the weekly repetition paragraph 2 says builds acquaintance.
qs.x: The author's test is repeated, compelled waiting among the same people, as described in paragraphs 2 and 3. Commuters at the same bus stop each weekday fit that exactly. A yearly festival is tempting as a neighborhood gathering, but it lacks the weekly repetition that turns nods into acquaintance.

qs.q: Which finding, if true, would most undermine the author's argument?
o: Cafés that replace laundromats charge higher prices than older businesses
Higher prices fit the author's point that chosen settings sort by income.
Laundromat users typically wear headphones and never speak to fellow customers
Correct: without exchanges, the web of acquaintance described in paragraph 2 never forms.
Residents rarely name laundromats when surveyed about valued places
Paragraph 4 predicts exactly this: such places go unnamed in surveys.
Some residents prefer in-unit machines to visiting a laundromat
The author grants that preference and does not argue against convenience.
qs.x: The argument depends on repeated waiting actually producing exchanges that build weak ties, as paragraph 2 describes. If users never speak, co-presence produces no web of acquaintance and the claimed value disappears. The survey choice is tempting, but paragraph 4 predicts that people will not name such places in surveys, so that finding fits the argument.

passages.title: What the Unbroken Shot Hides
text: Among critics who care about such things, there persists a moral hierarchy of film technique. The long take, a single shot that runs uncut for minutes, sits near the top: it is said to respect the spectator's freedom, to let time pass as it really passes, and to refuse the manipulation of editing. Montage, the rapid assembly of fragments, sits near the bottom, tainted by its association with propaganda and advertising. The long take is honest; the cut is a lie.

This hierarchy has a distinguished pedigree, but it confuses a style with a virtue. A long take is no less constructed than a montage sequence. Someone chose where the camera stands, what enters and leaves the frame, when the actors move and how long the shot will run before it ends. The absence of visible cuts does not remove the filmmaker's hand; it hides it. If anything, a carefully choreographed long take can be more coercive than editing, because the spectator, believing herself free to look wherever she likes, does not notice how thoroughly her attention has been steered by movement, light and sound.

Nor does montage necessarily deceive. A sequence that cuts between a factory owner's banquet and his workers' meager meal makes its argument openly. The juxtaposition announces itself; the viewer sees that a comparison is being made and can accept or reject it. Editing, in this sense, can be the more candid technique, since it wears its artifice on its surface.

None of this means that the long take lacks distinctive powers. Duration can produce effects nothing else can: the slow accumulation of tension, the boredom that turns into attention, the sense of a world continuing beyond the frame. My objection is only to the claim that these powers are ethical rather than aesthetic. Techniques do not carry morals within them. Honesty in film, as elsewhere, belongs to what is being said and to whether the speaker invites us to see how it is being said, not to the length of the sentences.

qs.q: The main purpose of the passage is to:
o: challenge the view that the long take is inherently more honest than editing
Correct: paragraph 2 says the hierarchy 'confuses a style with a virtue.'
argue that montage is aesthetically superior to the long take
Paragraph 4 credits the long take with powers 'nothing else can' produce.
trace the historical origins of montage in propaganda films
Propaganda is mentioned only in passing in paragraph 1.
explain the technical difficulty of filming a long take
The passage discusses ethics and style, not technical difficulty.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 states the thesis: the critical hierarchy 'confuses a style with a virtue,' so the long take is not inherently more honest than editing. Saying montage is aesthetically superior overshoots, because paragraph 4 grants the long take powers that nothing else can produce.

qs.q: The banquet example in paragraph 3 is used chiefly to illustrate that:
o: a cut can openly present a comparison the viewer is free to evaluate
Correct: paragraph 3 says the juxtaposition 'announces itself' so the viewer can accept or reject it.
montage is most effective when it depicts economic injustice
The author uses the example for its form, not to rank political subjects.
long takes cannot depict two locations at the same time
The passage never claims this limitation of the long take.
editing always manipulates viewers without their awareness
This is the opposite of the point; the example shows editing being candid.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 uses the banquet-versus-workers' meal cut to show that editing can be candid: the comparison 'announces itself,' and the viewer can accept or reject it. The tempting political reading misses that the example is about the form of the argument, not its subject.

qs.q: According to the author, why can a long take be 'more coercive' than editing?
o: Long takes are longer and therefore exhaust the viewer's critical faculties
The author attributes coercion to hidden steering, not to fatigue.
Viewers who feel free to look anywhere fail to notice how their gaze is directed
Correct: paragraph 2 says the spectator 'does not notice' how her attention is steered.
Long takes are mostly used in propaganda and advertising
Paragraph 1 links propaganda to montage, not to the long take.
Editing gives the viewer no choice about where to look
This would make editing more coercive, contrary to the author's point.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 says the long take hides the filmmaker's hand. A viewer who believes she is free to look anywhere does not notice how movement, light and sound steer her attention. The fatigue choice is tempting because long takes are long, but the passage blames hidden steering, not exhaustion.

qs.q: Which statement would the author be most likely to accept?
o: The long take produces no effects that editing cannot also achieve
Paragraph 4 says duration produces effects 'nothing else can.'
Ethical filmmakers should avoid visible cuts whenever possible
This restates the hierarchy the author rejects.
A documentary that cuts frequently can be more truthful than one that never cuts
Correct: paragraph 4 says honesty lies in what is said, not in shot length.
Film techniques carry inherent moral qualities apart from their use
Paragraph 4 states directly that 'techniques do not carry morals within them.'
qs.x: Paragraph 4 says honesty belongs to what is said and whether we are shown how it is said, not to technique, so a heavily cut documentary could be the more truthful one. Avoiding cuts restates the hierarchy the author rejects, and denying the long take any unique effects contradicts paragraph 4's list of its powers.

qs.q: Which analogy best reflects the author's reasoning about film technique?
o: A photograph is more honest than a painting because it involves no human choices
The author argues that even unedited images involve many human choices.
Handwritten letters are more sincere than typed ones because they show effort
This ties virtue to a technique, the very move the author rejects.
A live broadcast is more honest than a recording because it cannot be edited
This repeats the long-take hierarchy the author disputes.
Short sentences are not more truthful than long ones; truth depends on the content
Correct: the final sentence makes this exact comparison to 'the length of the sentences.'
qs.x: The final sentence of paragraph 4 compares shot length to 'the length of the sentences': truth depends on content, not form. An analogy saying short sentences are no more truthful than long ones matches this. The other choices all tie virtue to a technique, which is the reasoning the author attacks.

qs.q: A director makes a ten-minute uncut shot but adds an on-screen note explaining how each movement was rehearsed. How would the author most likely view this?
o: As destroying the long take's distinctive power of duration
A note does not shorten the shot or remove its accumulated duration.
As pointless, since long takes are already fully honest
The author denies that long takes are honest by nature.
As increasing the film's candor by showing how its effect is produced
Correct: paragraph 4 locates honesty in inviting us to see 'how it is being said.'
As turning the long take into a form of montage
Adding a note introduces no cuts or juxtaposition of fragments.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 places honesty partly in whether the filmmaker 'invites us to see how it is being said.' A note explaining the rehearsed movements does exactly that, so it makes the shot more candid. Calling it pointless assumes long takes are already honest, which paragraph 2 denies.

passages.title: The Arrow and the Opening
text: Ancient Greek had two words for time. Chronos was time as sequence, the steady march of hours that a water clock could measure. Kairos was time as opportunity, the moment when an action becomes fitting or possible. The word seems to have been used of archery, where it named the narrow gap through which an arrow must pass, and of weaving, where it named the instant when the shuttle can slip through the parted threads. For the teachers of rhetoric, kairos named something no handbook could fully capture: the sense of when to speak, what to say to these listeners in this mood, and when to stop.

Modern instruction in persuasive writing has largely abandoned this idea. Students learn templates: a thesis in the first paragraph, three supporting points, a counterargument, a conclusion that restates the thesis. Such templates have real uses. They make arguments easier to grade and give beginners a scaffold. But they presuppose that a good argument is good everywhere, that its quality is a property of its internal structure rather than of its fit to an occasion.

The older tradition knew better. Gorgias, one of the first professional teachers of rhetoric, reportedly delighted in speaking on any subject an audience proposed, and his showpieces suggest a man more interested in responsiveness than in fixed rules. Even Aristotle, who did more than anyone to systematize rhetoric, insisted that the available means of persuasion must be discovered anew in each case. His categories of appeal were tools for noticing what a situation offered, not formulas for producing speeches in advance.

To restore kairos to the classroom would not mean discarding structure. It would mean teaching students to ask, before they write, who will read this, what those readers already believe, what has just happened that makes the topic urgent or tired, and what would be the wrong thing to say now. These questions cannot be answered by a template, which is precisely why they are worth teaching. An argument that is correct but untimely persuades no one, and an archer who aims perfectly at a closed gap still misses.

qs.q: As the passage uses the term, kairos refers to:
o: the fitting or opportune moment for an action
Correct: paragraph 1 defines it as 'time as opportunity.'
time measured as a steady sequence of hours
Paragraph 1 assigns that meaning to chronos, not kairos.
a standard structure for organizing an argument
Templates are a modern practice the author contrasts with kairos.
Aristotle's list of the three types of appeal
Paragraph 3 mentions Aristotle's categories but does not call them kairos.
qs.x: Paragraph 1 contrasts two Greek words: chronos is measured sequence, while kairos is 'time as opportunity,' the fitting moment to act, like the gap an arrow must pass through. The main trap is swapping in chronos's definition, which appears in the same paragraph.

qs.q: The author's main criticism of writing templates is that they:
o: are too difficult for beginning writers to master
Paragraph 2 says templates give beginners a helpful scaffold.
make it harder for instructors to grade student essays
Paragraph 2 says templates make arguments easier to grade.
were invented by Gorgias and so reflect outdated thinking
Gorgias is presented as interested in responsiveness, not as inventing templates.
treat argumentative quality as independent of the audience and occasion
Correct: paragraph 2 says they presuppose quality is internal rather than fitted to an occasion.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 grants that templates help with grading and give beginners a scaffold. Its objection is that they assume an argument's quality lies in its internal structure, not in how it fits an occasion and audience. Two choices simply reverse the benefits the author concedes.

qs.q: The author refers to Aristotle in paragraph 3 most likely to show that:
o: Aristotle rejected Gorgias's interest in responding to audiences
No disagreement between the two is described.
even the great systematizer of rhetoric treated persuasion as situational
Correct: paragraph 3 says Aristotle held the means of persuasion must be discovered in each case.
systematic approaches to rhetoric inevitably fail
The author says Aristotle's categories were useful tools for noticing.
modern templates are directly derived from Aristotle's categories
The passage draws no line of descent from Aristotle to modern templates.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 calls Aristotle the thinker who did most to systematize rhetoric, yet says he held that the means of persuasion must be discovered 'anew in each case.' Using him shows that even system-building treated persuasion as situational. Saying systematic approaches inevitably fail overreaches, since his categories are described as useful tools.

qs.q: Which practice would best fit the author's proposal for restoring kairos to the classroom?
o: Requiring every essay to place its thesis in the first sentence
This is a fixed template rule, the approach the author critiques.
Having students rewrite one argument for two audiences with different prior beliefs
Correct: paragraph 4 urges asking who will read and what they already believe.
Grading essays solely on grammar and spelling
Mechanical correctness ignores the occasion and audience entirely.
Having students memorize famous ancient speeches word for word
Memorization reproduces past speeches rather than fitting new occasions.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 urges students to ask who will read a piece, what those readers already believe, and what would be wrong to say now. Rewriting one argument for two audiences with different beliefs puts those questions into practice. Memorizing ancient speeches seems true to the classical tradition but copies past occasions instead of fitting new ones.

qs.q: A speechwriter delivers a well-argued case for a budget cut the day after a disaster that the cut would have worsened, and the audience reacts with anger. The author would most likely explain the failure as:
o: proof that the argument's structure was logically flawed
The scenario stipulates a well-argued case; the author separates timing from structure.
evidence that audiences cannot be persuaded by reasoned argument
The author thinks timely arguments can persuade; the issue is fit, not reason.
a result of following Aristotle's categories too closely
The author presents Aristotle's categories as tools for noticing situations.
a failure of timing, regardless of the argument's internal quality
Correct: paragraph 4 says a correct but untimely argument 'persuades no one.'
qs.x: The case is stipulated as well argued, so its structure is not the problem; it came at the worst possible moment. Paragraph 4 says a correct but untimely argument 'persuades no one,' like an archer aiming at a closed gap. The logic-flaw choice ignores that the author treats internal quality and timing as separate.

passages.title: No Garden to Return To
text: Ecological restoration rests on a seductive picture. Somewhere in the past there was an intact ecosystem; human activity degraded it; our task is to put it back. The restorer studies old surveys, pollen cores and early travelers' accounts to reconstruct the baseline, then works to reproduce it, removing the newcomers and reintroducing the vanished.

The difficulty is that there is no single past to return to. Every landscape has been changing continuously, through shifting climates, migrating species and, for thousands of years in most places, the burning, hunting and planting of earlier human inhabitants. Choosing a baseline therefore means choosing one moment from a moving film and declaring it the authentic frame. In practice the chosen moment often coincides with the arrival of the first literate observers, which quietly treats earlier peoples' long management of the land as part of nature while treating later human influence as contamination. That choice is not a scientific finding. It is a value judgment, and often a politically loaded one.

Moreover, the conditions that sustained a historical ecosystem may no longer exist. Where the climate has warmed, a species assemblage recreated from a century ago may be unable to persist without perpetual intervention. Restoration then becomes a kind of museum curation: admirable perhaps, but a different project from letting nature flourish.

None of this licenses indifference. The alternative to a fixed baseline is not to accept whatever damage occurs, but to shift the question from what a place was to what it is capable of becoming. We can ask whether a landscape is resilient, whether it supports a diversity of life, whether its processes, such as flooding, fire and seed dispersal, function without constant human rescue. These are criteria about trajectories rather than snapshots. They allow that a healthy future ecosystem might include species that were never there before and lack some that once were.
Such a view will disappoint those who want restoration to be an act of atonement, a returning of what was taken. But atonement looks backward, and ecosystems do not.

qs.q: The author's main objection to baseline-oriented restoration is that:
o: there is no uniquely authentic past state for a landscape to be returned to
Correct: paragraph 2 says 'there is no single past to return to.'
restoration projects cost too much relative to their benefits
Cost is never discussed in the passage.
pollen cores and old surveys are unreliable sources of data
The author mentions these sources without questioning their reliability.
humans should never intervene in natural processes
Paragraph 4 rejects indifference and accepts intervention guided by new criteria.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 says 'there is no single past to return to,' since landscapes change constantly. Picking any baseline therefore freezes one frame of a moving film. The anti-intervention choice is tempting, but paragraph 4 explicitly rejects indifference and endorses intervention guided by other criteria.

qs.q: The author suggests that choosing the arrival of literate observers as a baseline is problematic mainly because it:
o: relies on written accounts that tend to exaggerate wildlife abundance
The passage does not question the accuracy of early accounts.
ignores the effects of climate change on future species survival
Climate is discussed in paragraph 3 as a separate problem, not this one.
implicitly counts earlier human land management as natural and later influence as damage
Correct: paragraph 2 says this choice treats earlier peoples' management as 'part of nature.'
is too recent to show what the landscape looked like before humans
The author's point is about inconsistency in judging human influence, not age.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 says choosing the moment literate observers arrived quietly counts earlier peoples' land management as nature and later human influence as contamination, an inconsistent value judgment. The climate choice is tempting because it is a real problem in the passage, but it belongs to paragraph 3 as a separate objection.

qs.q: In the context of paragraph 3, 'museum curation' implies that some restorations:
o: are designed mainly to educate visitors about history
Paragraph 3 says nothing about visitors or education.
are worthless and should be abandoned immediately
The author calls such curation 'admirable perhaps,' not worthless.
succeed in recreating self-sustaining natural processes
Curation is contrasted with letting nature flourish on its own.
preserve a historical arrangement only through ongoing human effort
Correct: paragraph 3 says such assemblages may not persist 'without perpetual intervention.'
qs.x: Paragraph 3 says a recreated assemblage may not survive 'without perpetual intervention.' Calling restoration museum curation means the historical arrangement is kept on display only by constant human upkeep. 'Admirable perhaps' rules out reading it as worthless, and curation is contrasted with self-sustaining nature.

qs.q: Which project would best meet the author's preferred criteria for ecological health?
o: Removing every species not recorded in an 1850 land survey
This applies the fixed historical baseline the author critiques.
Fencing a meadow and leaving all human damage untouched
Paragraph 4 says the alternative is not to accept whatever damage occurs.
Restoring seasonal floods to a river plain even if some non-native species remain
Correct: paragraph 4 values functioning processes such as flooding over a historical snapshot.
Replanting a forest exactly as an early explorer's drawings show it
This is snapshot restoration based on a chosen past moment.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 asks whether processes such as flooding, fire and seed dispersal work without constant rescue, and it accepts species that were never there before. Restoring seasonal floods despite some non-native species fits this best. Removing species missing from an 1850 survey or copying an explorer's drawings both use the fixed baseline the author criticizes.

qs.q: Suppose researchers found that a recreated historical grassland persisted for decades without any human management despite a warming climate. This finding would:
o: refute the author's argument that baselines involve value judgments
Persistence says nothing about whether choosing the baseline was a value judgment.
weaken the claim in paragraph 3 for that case, without undermining paragraph 2
Correct: it counters the persistence worry but not the point that any baseline is a value choice.
strengthen the author's claim that historical assemblages need intervention
It shows the opposite: the assemblage persisted without intervention.
support the view that restoration should be an act of atonement
Ecological persistence does not bear on the moral framing of atonement.
qs.x: Paragraph 3's worry is that historical assemblages may not last under new conditions. A grassland that persists unaided weakens that worry for this case. Paragraph 2's separate claim, that picking a baseline is a value judgment, concerns how goals are chosen, so ecological success leaves it untouched.

qs.q: The final paragraph's contrast between atonement and ecosystems implies that:
o: restoration goals should be set by future possibilities, not by restoring the past
Correct: since 'ecosystems do not' look backward, goals should concern trajectories.
humans owe no moral debt for past environmental harm
The author questions a backward-looking framing, not whether harm was done.
ecosystems recover faster when humans feel guilt
No causal link between guilt and recovery is suggested.
atonement is the most widely held motive for restoration
The author says some hold this view but makes no claim about how common it is.
qs.x: Paragraph 5 says atonement 'looks backward, and ecosystems do not,' which echoes paragraph 4's call to judge places by trajectories rather than snapshots. The no-moral-debt choice is tempting but too strong: the author questions a backward-looking way of setting goals, not whether past harm happened.

passages.title: Bodies as Archives
text: For most of its history, choreography has survived the way gossip survives: by being passed from one person to another. A dancer learns a role from someone who danced it before, who learned it from someone earlier still. Each link in the chain adds a little and loses a little. By the time a ballet reaches its fifth or sixth generation of performers, no one can say with certainty how it looked on the night it premiered.

To many observers this has seemed a scandal. Music has its scores and drama its scripts; why should dance alone be condemned to forgetting? The twentieth century produced several ambitious answers, most famously the notation system devised by Rudolf Laban, which records the direction, level, duration and body part of every movement on a vertical staff. Trained notators can reconstruct a work from such a score decades after its last performance, and some lost dances have been recovered this way.

I admire these systems, but I doubt that they solve the problem their champions believe they solve. A score records what a body does; it does not record how it feels to do it, or which of a thousand small qualities the choreographer cared about most. When a dancer learns a role from a predecessor, she receives not only the steps but a set of priorities: this arm matters, that turn can be loosened, the stillness before the leap is the point of the whole phrase. A notated score treats every element as equally essential, and in doing so it can preserve the letter of a dance while losing its emphasis.

There is also a deeper sense in which the chain of bodies is not a defect but the medium itself. A dance that changes slightly with each generation is not being corrupted; it is being kept alive, the way a language is kept alive by speakers who bend it. Notation can serve as a valuable check, a way of noticing when drift has gone too far. But a dance that exists only on paper is closer to a dead language than to a preserved one: legible, perhaps, yet no longer spoken.

qs.q: According to the passage, Laban's notation system records all of the following EXCEPT:
o: how a movement feels to the dancer performing it
Correct: paragraph 3 says a score 'does not record how it feels to do it.'
the direction of each movement
Paragraph 2 lists direction among the elements Laban notation records.
the duration of each movement
Paragraph 2 lists duration among the recorded elements.
the body part performing each movement
Paragraph 2 lists body part among the recorded elements.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 lists what Laban notation records: direction, level, duration and body part of every movement. Paragraph 3 then says a score 'does not record how it feels to do it.' For an EXCEPT question, check each choice against the list; the three listed features are all named in paragraph 2.

qs.q: The author's central concern about notated scores is that they:
o: cannot be read by anyone except the original choreographer
Paragraph 2 says trained notators can reconstruct works decades later.
fail to convey which elements of a dance matter most
Correct: paragraph 3 says a score treats every element as equally essential, losing emphasis.
have never succeeded in recovering a lost dance
Paragraph 2 says some lost dances have been recovered this way.
introduce more errors than person-to-person teaching does
The author never compares error rates; the issue is lost priorities.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 says a dancer learning in person receives priorities (this arm matters, that turn can be loosened), while a score treats every element as equally essential and so loses emphasis. The legibility and failure choices are contradicted by paragraph 2, which says notators reconstruct and recover works.

qs.q: The comparison of dance to a language in paragraph 4 suggests that the author views generational change in a dance as:
o: a regrettable loss that notation should eliminate
The author says the chain of bodies is 'not a defect but the medium itself.'
proof that dances have no stable identity at all
The author treats change as slight and calls notation a check on excessive drift.
a sign of continued life rather than of decay
Correct: paragraph 4 says such a dance 'is being kept alive' like a language bent by speakers.
unimportant compared with the accuracy of the original premiere
The author does not prize premiere accuracy over a living tradition.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 says a dance that changes with each generation 'is being kept alive,' the way speakers keep a language alive by bending it. So change signals life, not decay. Saying dances have no stable identity overreaches, because the author still wants notation as a check on drift that goes too far.

qs.q: Which statement best describes the author's overall position on dance notation?
o: It should replace person-to-person teaching wherever possible
The author argues the opposite, that bodies are the medium itself.
It is worthless because it cannot capture any aspect of dance
The author says 'I admire these systems' and that they record what a body does.
It is superior to musical scores in what it can preserve
No ranking of dance notation against musical scores is offered.
It is a useful supplement to transmission between bodies, not a replacement for it
Correct: paragraph 4 calls it 'a valuable check' while insisting the chain of bodies is the medium.
qs.x: The author admires notation and calls it 'a valuable check' on drift (paragraphs 3 and 4) but insists the chain of bodies is the medium itself, so notation supplements live transmission and cannot replace it. Calling it worthless ignores the stated admiration, and making it a replacement reverses the thesis.

qs.q: Which situation is most analogous to the author's concern about notated dance?
o: A photograph that fades over many years in sunlight
Fading is physical decay, not the loss of emphasis the author describes.
A song performed in a key different from the original
A key change alters content openly; it is not a record that flattens priorities.
A family recipe written down without the cook's sense of which steps truly matter
Correct: like a score, the recipe keeps the steps but loses the priorities passed in person.
A novel translated into many languages for new readers
Translation is closer to the living adaptation the author approves of.
qs.x: The author's worry is a record that keeps every step while losing the in-person sense of which steps matter most. A recipe written down without the cook's priorities has the same flaw. Translation is tempting as a kind of transmission, but it is closer to the living adaptation the author approves of in paragraph 4.

qs.q: A company stages a ballet solely from a notated score, with no dancer who learned it in person. Audiences who saw an earlier version say the steps are right but the piece feels flat. This report would:
o: support the author's claim that scores keep the letter but lose the emphasis
Correct: correct steps without the felt priorities is exactly the loss paragraph 3 predicts.
weaken the author's claim that notation can recover lost dances
The steps were recovered; the author never claimed scores preserve emphasis.
show that notation records nothing accurately
The audience says the steps are right, so the score was accurate on its own terms.
prove that the dance had drifted too far from the original
The problem stems from the score, not from generational drift.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 predicts that a score can 'preserve the letter of a dance while losing its emphasis.' Correct steps with a flat feel is exactly that outcome, so the report supports the author. It does not weaken the recovery claim in paragraph 2, because the steps were in fact recovered; only the emphasis was missing.

passages.title: Hot Iron and Reasonable Doubt
text: Few legal practices strike modern readers as more absurd than the medieval ordeal. An accused person might be made to carry a red-hot iron for several paces or plunge an arm into boiling water; if the wound healed cleanly after a few days, God had declared the person innocent. It is tempting to treat such procedures as pure superstition, a grim curiosity from an age before reason. I want to suggest that they were, within their world, a surprisingly shrewd solution to a problem every legal system faces.

That problem is what to do when evidence runs out. Where there were no witnesses and no confession, early medieval courts had few tools for discovering the truth. The ordeal was reserved for exactly such cases. Crucially, it worked through the beliefs of the accused. Someone who believed that God would reveal guilt had strong reason to confess or settle before ever touching the iron, while an innocent person, confident of vindication, had reason to proceed. The ordeal thus sorted defendants by their own expectations, and the mere prospect of it may have extracted many confessions from the guilty.

Records also suggest that a surprisingly large share of those who underwent the ordeal were cleared. One plausible explanation is that the priests who administered it had considerable discretion, over how hot the iron was, how long it was held and how a healing wound was judged, and may have tended to exonerate those who had shown willingness to proceed. If so, the ordeal was not blind chance but a ritual whose outcome reflected a reasonable inference: those willing to face it were probably innocent.

The system depended entirely on shared belief, and that is why it collapsed. In 1215 the Fourth Lateran Council forbade clergy to take part in ordeals, partly from theological doubts about demanding miracles of God. Without priests, the ritual lost its authority. English courts turned increasingly to juries of neighbors, a change usually told as progress. Perhaps it was. But we should notice that the jury, too, is a device for producing a verdict when certainty is unavailable, and that it, too, rests on a shared faith, in this case faith in the judgment of ordinary people.

qs.q: According to the passage, ordeals were typically used when:
o: the accused was a member of the clergy
The passage says priests administered ordeals, not that they were the accused.
a jury of neighbors could not agree on a verdict
Paragraph 4 says juries came after ordeals were abandoned.
the crime carried the death penalty
The passage never ties the ordeal to the severity of punishment.
no witnesses or confession were available to settle the case
Correct: paragraph 2 says the ordeal was reserved for cases where evidence ran out.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 says ordeals were reserved for cases where evidence ran out: no witnesses and no confession. The jury choice reverses the sequence, because paragraph 4 presents juries as what replaced ordeals after 1215.

qs.q: The author's argument that the ordeal 'sorted defendants by their own expectations' depends on the assumption that:
o: priests were indifferent to the outcome of each ordeal
Paragraph 3 suggests priests used discretion, so indifference is not assumed.
most accused persons sincerely believed God would reveal the truth
Correct: paragraph 2's sorting works only if the accused shared that belief.
guilty people were physically less able to endure pain
The mechanism concerns belief and choice, not pain tolerance.
juries would have reached the same verdicts as ordeals
The argument about sorting does not depend on any comparison to juries.
qs.x: The sorting described in paragraph 2 works only if the accused actually expect God to reveal guilt: the guilty then confess or settle, while the innocent proceed confidently. Without that belief, defendants would have no reason to sort themselves. The priest-indifference choice fails because paragraph 3 suggests priests used discretion.

qs.q: Which evidence from the passage best supports the claim that ordeal outcomes reflected 'a reasonable inference' rather than chance?
o: The Fourth Lateran Council forbade clergy participation in 1215
This explains the ordeal's end, not how its outcomes were reached.
A large share of those who underwent the ordeal were cleared
Correct: paragraph 3 links frequent acquittals to priests' discretion favoring the willing.
The accused might carry a red-hot iron for several paces
This describes the procedure, not evidence about its outcomes.
English courts later turned to juries of neighbors
This concerns the successor system, not the logic of ordeal verdicts.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 reasons from the high acquittal rate: priests with discretion likely cleared those who had shown willingness to proceed, so outcomes tracked a sensible inference instead of chance. The 1215 council and the later juries concern how the system ended, not how verdicts were reached.

qs.q: The author's attitude toward the replacement of ordeals by juries is best described as:
o: enthusiastic, viewing juries as wholly rational
The author stresses that juries also rest on faith.
hostile, arguing that ordeals were more accurate than juries
The author never claims ordeals were more accurate.
indifferent, treating the change as unimportant
The author draws a pointed parallel, which shows interest, not indifference.
cautious, granting it may be progress while noting a shared similarity
Correct: paragraph 4 says 'Perhaps it was' and then notes the jury also rests on shared faith.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 says the move to juries is 'usually told as progress' and answers 'Perhaps it was,' a hedge, before noting that juries also rest on shared faith. That is cautious, qualified acceptance. The hostile choice overreaches, since the author never claims ordeals were more accurate than juries.

qs.q: Which modern practice works most like the mechanism the author attributes to the ordeal?
o: A lie-detector test whose main value is that suspects who believe it works confess beforehand
Correct: like the ordeal in paragraph 2, it works through the suspect's belief in its power.
A DNA test that matches crime-scene samples to a suspect
DNA evidence works independently of what the suspect believes.
A jury trial in which twelve citizens weigh the evidence
The author presents juries as a successor system relying on faith in ordinary judgment.
A judge's sentencing guidelines based on prior convictions
Sentencing guidelines do not elicit confessions through the defendant's beliefs.
qs.x: The ordeal's power in paragraph 2 came through the suspect's belief, which pushed the guilty to confess before the test. A lie detector valued mainly because believing suspects confess beforehand works the same way. DNA testing is tempting as a modern truth-finding tool, but it works no matter what the suspect believes.

passages.title: The Road Is the Relic
text: Scholars of religion have long been uneasy about the line between pilgrimage and tourism. The pilgrim, we are told, travels to a sacred place to encounter something holy; the tourist travels to see something interesting. One journey is devotion, the other is consumption. The distinction feels obvious until one tries to apply it. The medieval travelers to Santiago de Compostela bought badges, haggled at inns, complained about food and gossiped about their companions. Many modern hikers on the same route profess no faith at all, yet describe the walk as the most spiritually significant experience of their lives.

The trouble, I think, is that the conventional distinction locates the meaning of pilgrimage at its destination. If the point is to reach the shrine and venerate the relic, then a traveler's beliefs about the shrine determine whether the trip counts as religious. But many pilgrims, past and present, describe the destination almost as an afterthought. What they remember is the blistered feet, the strangers who shared bread, the slow surrender of ordinary routine. The arrival is often anticlimactic; the transformation, if it comes, happens along the way.

If the road rather than the relic carries the meaning, the line between pilgrim and tourist must be drawn differently, if at all. The difference would lie not in what one believes about the destination, but in how one undergoes the journey: whether one submits to its hardships and uncertainties or insulates oneself from them. A devout believer who is driven to the cathedral door in an air-conditioned coach may be more of a tourist, in this sense, than an unbelieving walker who has slept in church porches for a month.

This reframing has a cost, and I do not want to hide it. It risks dissolving the specifically religious content of pilgrimage into a generic language of self-discovery, available equally to marathon runners and backpackers. Traditional pilgrims would hardly accept that their faith was incidental. Still, the reframing captures something the conventional view misses: that in many traditions the sacred is approached through the body and through time, and that the effort of approach is itself a form of devotion.

qs.q: The author's main point is that the meaning of pilgrimage lies chiefly in:
o: the traveler's beliefs about the sacred destination
This is the conventional view the author argues against in paragraph 2.
the relic venerated at the end of the route
The author says the destination is often 'almost an afterthought.'
the experience of undergoing the journey itself
Correct: paragraph 2 says the transformation 'happens along the way.'
the badges and souvenirs bought along the route
These are mentioned in paragraph 1 to blur the pilgrim–tourist line, not as the meaning.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 argues that the conventional view wrongly places pilgrimage's meaning at the destination. Pilgrims remember the journey, and 'the transformation, if it comes, happens along the way.' The belief-about-destination choice is the view being criticized, not the author's own.

qs.q: The details about medieval travelers in paragraph 1 are offered mainly to:
o: prove that medieval pilgrims lacked genuine faith
The author does not question their faith; the point concerns behavior.
explain why Santiago de Compostela became a famous shrine
The passage gives no account of the shrine's rise to fame.
argue that modern hikers are more spiritual than medieval travelers
No such ranking is made; both groups illustrate the blurred line.
show that past pilgrims also behaved in ways we associate with tourism
Correct: buying badges and haggling make the 'obvious' distinction hard to apply.
qs.x: Paragraph 1 says the pilgrim–tourist line 'feels obvious until one tries to apply it,' then shows medieval pilgrims buying badges, haggling and gossiping like tourists. The details blur the line; they do not question anyone's faith. No ranking of modern hikers against medieval travelers is made.

qs.q: Under the author's reframing, which traveler would most clearly count as a tourist rather than a pilgrim?
o: A nonbeliever who walks the route for weeks sleeping in porches
Paragraph 3 suggests this walker may be more of a pilgrim than a comfortable believer.
A believer who walks the route and finds the arrival anticlimactic
Paragraph 2 says anticlimactic arrival is common among genuine pilgrims.
A believer who reaches the shrine in comfort while avoiding every hardship
Correct: paragraph 3 defines the difference by whether one insulates oneself from the journey.
A walker who shares bread with strangers along the way
Sharing with strangers is among the experiences pilgrims remember in paragraph 2.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 redraws the line by how one undergoes the journey: whether one submits to its hardships or insulates oneself from them. A believer who reaches the shrine in comfort while avoiding every hardship is the clearest tourist. Belief is the tempting criterion, but under this reframing it no longer decides the matter.

qs.q: What 'cost' of the reframing does the author acknowledge in paragraph 4?
o: It makes pilgrimage more physically dangerous for travelers
The cost described is conceptual, not physical.
It may reduce pilgrimage's religious content to generic self-discovery
Correct: paragraph 4 warns it risks dissolving religious content into self-discovery language.
It would reduce the number of people walking pilgrimage routes
The passage makes no prediction about numbers of walkers.
It requires scholars to stop studying pilgrimage altogether
The author proposes redrawing the distinction, not ending study.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 openly admits the reframing 'risks dissolving the specifically religious content of pilgrimage' into generic self-discovery talk that marathon runners could share. The cost is conceptual: a loss of religious specificity. It is not physical danger or fewer walkers.

qs.q: Which new finding would most strengthen the author's argument?
o: Interviews showing pilgrims recall the walk far more vividly than their arrival
Correct: this supports paragraph 2's claim that meaning lies in the road, not the relic.
Records showing shrines attracted more visitors when relics were displayed
This would emphasize the destination's pull, cutting against the author's view.
Surveys showing most modern walkers are religious believers
Belief about the destination is what the author thinks matters less.
Evidence that medieval inns along the route were expensive
Inn prices do not bear on where pilgrimage's meaning lies.
qs.x: The author's claim is that meaning lives in the road, not the relic (paragraph 2). Interviews showing that pilgrims recall the walk far more vividly than the arrival would directly support it. Evidence that displayed relics drew more visitors stresses the destination's pull and cuts the other way.

passages.title: Reading the Rubbish Heap
text: The public imagines archaeology as a search for treasure: gold masks, painted tombs, the palaces of kings. Practicing archaeologists know that their most informative finds usually come from somewhere far less glamorous. A midden, the heap where a household or village dumped its refuse, can reveal what people ate, which animals they kept, what tools broke and were discarded, and how all of this changed over generations, layer upon layer.

The great virtue of garbage is that it was not meant to be seen. A monument is a message composed for an audience, often for posterity; it tells us what its builders wished to be remembered for. A trash heap tells us what they actually did. A king's inscription may boast of plenty while the village midden from the same decade fills with the bones of animals that were eaten only in famine. Where the two disagree, the archaeologist has good reason to trust the rubbish.

Yet garbage has biases of its own, and they are easy to forget precisely because no one intended them. Bone, pottery and stone survive for thousands of years; wood, textiles, leather and most plant foods rot within decades unless conditions are unusually dry, cold or waterlogged. A midden may therefore suggest a diet dominated by meat and shellfish simply because those remains endure while the grains, roots and greens that fed people daily have vanished. The absence of evidence in a trash heap is often evidence only of decay.

The lesson is not that rubbish is unreliable but that its honesty is of a particular kind. It is free from the distortions of intention but not from the distortions of chemistry. A careful archaeologist reads a midden the way a careful historian reads a chronicle: alert to what the source could not have recorded, as well as to what it does. Modern techniques, from sieving for tiny seeds to analyzing chemical residues in pottery, have begun to recover some of what decay erased. But the first discipline remains a habit of mind, the refusal to mistake what has survived for what once existed.

qs.q: According to the passage, why might a midden overrepresent meat in an ancient diet?
o: Bones survive far longer than most plant remains
Correct: paragraph 3 says bone endures while grains, roots and greens rot.
Ancient people deliberately buried plant waste elsewhere
The passage attributes the bias to decay, not to intentional disposal.
Kings exaggerated meat consumption in their inscriptions
Inscriptions are discussed separately; they do not shape midden contents.
Archaeologists have historically ignored animal bones
If they ignored bones, meat would be underrepresented, not overrepresented.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 explains the bias as uneven decay: bone, pottery and stone last thousands of years, while grains, roots and greens rot. So meat looks dominant only because its remains survive. The choice about archaeologists ignoring bones would make meat look scarcer, the opposite effect.

qs.q: The author contrasts a king's inscription with a village midden (paragraph 2) in order to show that:
o: inscriptions are always false while middens are always true
Paragraph 3 says middens have their own biases, so neither is always reliable.
unintended remains can correct the self-presentation of deliberate records
Correct: paragraph 2 says the trash tells what people did, the monument what they wished remembered.
famines were more common than historians once believed
The famine example is hypothetical and illustrates source conflict, not frequency.
villages kept better records than royal courts
A midden is not a record anyone kept; the point is its lack of intention.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 says a monument shows what its builders wanted remembered, while a trash heap shows what they actually did. Where they conflict, the unintended rubbish can correct the official story. 'Always true' overreaches, since paragraph 3 says middens have biases of their own.

qs.q: The author's statement that rubbish is free from 'the distortions of intention but not from the distortions of chemistry' means that middens:
o: were deliberately arranged to mislead later archaeologists
This would be a distortion of intention, which the author says middens lack.
can only be studied using modern chemical analysis
Chemistry here refers to decay, and paragraph 4 calls the first discipline a habit of mind.
are not shaped by a wish to impress yet are filtered by unequal preservation
Correct: paragraph 4 contrasts the absence of intent with the decay described in paragraph 3.
contain toxic substances that endanger excavators
The phrase concerns preservation bias, not physical hazards.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 says rubbish is free from 'the distortions of intention' (no one composed it to impress) but not from 'the distortions of chemistry,' meaning the uneven decay of paragraph 3. The deliberate-arrangement choice describes a distortion of intention, which middens lack.

qs.q: Which situation best illustrates the 'habit of mind' the author recommends?
o: Concluding that a site's people ate no vegetables because none were found
This treats absence from decay as real absence, the error paragraph 3 warns against.
Trusting a royal inscription over a midden because it is written
Paragraph 2 says the archaeologist has reason to trust the rubbish where they disagree.
Excavating only tombs because they contain the most valuable artifacts
The author says the most informative finds come from middens, not treasure.
Concluding that a lack of wooden tools at a dry-rotted site does not prove none were used
Correct: it refuses to mistake what survived for what existed, as paragraph 4 urges.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 names the habit: 'the refusal to mistake what has survived for what once existed.' Declining to conclude that no wooden tools were used at a site where wood rots shows that habit. Concluding that people ate no vegetables because none were found is the very error paragraph 3 warns about.

qs.q: At a waterlogged site, excavators find a midden full of preserved seeds and textile fragments. Compared with a typical dry midden, this site would most likely:
o: show a diet more dominated by meat and shellfish
Preserving plants would reduce, not increase, the apparent dominance of meat.
be less useful because it lacks a deliberate message
All middens lack deliberate messages; the author counts this as a virtue.
give a more complete picture of daily plant use and material life
Correct: paragraph 3 says waterlogged conditions can preserve normally perishable remains.
contradict the claim that garbage was not meant to be seen
Preservation conditions have nothing to do with the original intent behind refuse.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 says perishable remains survive only in unusually dry, cold or waterlogged conditions. A waterlogged midden that keeps seeds and textiles therefore offsets the usual preservation bias and gives a fuller picture of plant use and material life. Its plant remains would make meat look less dominant, not more.

passages.title: In Defense of the Lecture
text: It has become an article of faith in education circles that the lecture is obsolete. The image of one person talking while hundreds take notes is held up as the very picture of passive learning, a relic to be replaced by group projects, discussion and problem-solving. There is good evidence that students who actively work through material retain more than students who merely listen, and I do not dispute it. I dispute the conclusion that the lecture has nothing to offer.

The case against the lecture usually treats it as a delivery system for information, and judged that way it does look inefficient. A textbook can deliver the same facts more quickly, and a student can reread a page but not a spoken sentence. But the best lectures were never mainly about information. What a good lecturer offers is a demonstration of a mind at work: how an expert frames a question, which details she treats as important and which she sets aside, where she hesitates, what she finds surprising. These are precisely the things a textbook, with its finished and confident prose, conceals.

Seen this way, the lecture is less like a broadcast than like an apprenticeship conducted at scale. A novice carpenter learns by watching a master as well as by practicing; the watching teaches what to attend to. Students who never see an expert reason aloud must reconstruct that hidden judgment on their own, and many never manage it. Group work among novices can produce lively discussion while leaving everyone's misconceptions intact.

Nothing here excuses the dreary lecture, read from notes in a monotone, that gives the format its bad name. Nor does it argue against active learning, which is plainly valuable. The point is that the two serve different purposes and are better combined than opposed. Students need to practice, but they also need models of what skilled practice looks like. A lecture that thinks aloud, that shows its reasoning rather than merely reporting conclusions, is one of the few ways to provide such models to many people at once. Abolishing it in the name of activity would be like closing the workshop and leaving the apprentices to teach one another.

qs.q: According to the author, the chief value of a good lecture is that it:
o: shows students how an expert reasons through a problem
Correct: paragraph 2 calls it 'a demonstration of a mind at work.'
delivers factual information more efficiently than a textbook
Paragraph 2 concedes a textbook delivers facts more quickly.
allows students to reread material they did not understand
Paragraph 2 says a student can reread a page but not a spoken sentence.
replaces the need for students to practice on their own
Paragraph 4 says students still need to practice.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 says the best lectures were never mainly about information but offer 'a demonstration of a mind at work': how an expert frames questions and weighs details. The efficiency choice is tempting, but the author concedes a textbook delivers facts faster, so that cannot be the lecture's chief value.

qs.q: How does the author treat the evidence that active learning improves retention?
o: Rejects it as based on flawed studies
The author explicitly accepts the evidence.
Uses it to argue that lectures should be abolished
The author argues against abolishing lectures.
Ignores it in favor of personal experience
The author addresses the evidence directly in paragraph 1.
Accepts it but denies that it shows lectures are worthless
Correct: paragraph 1 says 'I do not dispute it' but disputes the conclusion drawn.
qs.x: Paragraph 1 says of the active-learning evidence, 'I do not dispute it,' then rejects the conclusion that lectures have nothing to offer. Accepting evidence while denying an inference drawn from it is a common CARS move. Using the evidence to abolish lectures is the opponents' view, not the author's.

qs.q: The carpenter analogy in paragraph 3 is meant to suggest that:
o: practical trades should be taught by lecture rather than by practice
The analogy credits both watching and practicing.
watching skilled practice teaches learners what to pay attention to
Correct: paragraph 3 says 'the watching teaches what to attend to.'
novices learn best when left to discover methods on their own
The author argues that unaided novices often fail to reconstruct expert judgment.
lectures are useful only for teaching manual skills
The analogy is applied to academic lectures, not limited to manual skills.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 says a novice carpenter learns by watching as well as practicing, because 'the watching teaches what to attend to.' Applied to lectures, students who watch an expert reason learn what to notice. The discovery-learning choice reverses the point: unaided novices often fail to reconstruct expert judgment.

qs.q: The author's claim about group work among novices (paragraph 3) supports the argument by suggesting that:
o: group work is less valuable than any form of lecture
Paragraph 4 says active learning is plainly valuable and should be combined.
activity alone cannot supply the expert models that correct misconceptions
Correct: discussion that leaves misconceptions intact shows the need for expert models.
students dislike working with classmates
Student preferences are not discussed.
discussion is always less lively than a lecture
Paragraph 3 says group work can produce lively discussion.

qs.q: Suppose a study found that students taught by lecturers who explained their reasoning made no fewer errors on new problems than students taught by lecturers who only stated conclusions. This would:
o: weaken the claim that seeing expert reasoning helps learners acquire judgment
Correct: the author's case rests on modeled reasoning transferring to students.
strengthen the claim that lectures are mainly delivery systems for facts
The study shows modeling had no added effect; it does not show what lectures are for.
support the author's call to combine lectures with active learning
The study does not test active learning, so it cannot support combining them.
have no bearing on the author's argument
It directly tests the mechanism the author credits for the lecture's value.
qs.x: The author's case rests on a mechanism: watching an expert reason aloud passes judgment on to students (paragraphs 2 and 3). If modeled reasoning produced no fewer errors on new problems, that mechanism is undercut. 'No bearing' fails because the study tests exactly the effect the argument relies on.
